title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
← Back to Trigger Lab
The Trigger Lab lets you design a parametric cyclone cover for Mozambique: pick a place, a radius and a wind speed, and see in which seasons since 1979/80 it would have paid, and how that matches the seasons that hurt. This article takes it apart: what each piece does, the code that does it, the ideas behind it, what it cannot tell, and what to read to go further.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
A trigger, not a claim
An ordinary insurance pays after someone has counted the damage. A parametric cover pays when something measured crosses a line agreed in advance: a wind speed, a rainfall total, a modelled loss. That makes it fast, because nobody has to count anything first. The price of that speed is that the measurement is not the loss. The cover can pay when little was lost, or stay silent when a lot was. That gap is called basis risk.
Index insurance of this kind is also used in farming: Barnett and Mahul (2007) describe weather index products for agriculture in lower-income countries and what they need to work. The Trigger Lab uses the simplest trigger there is, one storm, one wind speed, one zone, so that every part of the gap can be seen.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
Four outcomes
In any season, two questions have yes-or-no answers: did the trigger pay, and was there a disaster? That makes four outcomes (Figure 1).






Figure 1: The four outcomes of a trigger in one season. Basis risk is the two cells off the diagonal.



This is the same table that weather forecasters use to check a yes-or-no forecast: a forecast of rain against whether it rained. The parallel is more than a picture. A trigger is a forecast of loss made from a hazard measurement, and it can be judged the way forecasts are. Murphy (1993) separates three kinds of goodness in a forecast: consistency, quality (how well forecasts match what was observed) and value (what a decision maker gains by using them). The Trigger Lab shows quality, the four counts. It does not show value: what a miss costs a government against what a false alarm costs in premium.
Figueiredo et al. (2018) take the parallel further. A trigger that answers only yes or no, they argue, is open to basis risk; they propose triggers that give a probability of loss instead, and judge them with the tools of forecast verification. The Trigger Lab stays with yes or no, on purpose: it is the version a reader can hold in their head.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
The storms
The storms come from IBTrACS (Knapp et al. 2010), the archive that gathers the best tracks of all the agencies that watch tropical cyclones. For the South Indian Ocean it holds, among others, the tracks of the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center and of the regional centre on La Réunion. The page uses only the US columns: USA_LAT, USA_LON and USA_WIND. Two reasons:

One way of measuring wind. According to IBTrACS’ column documentation, agencies average the wind over different times: the US agencies over one minute, others over three or ten. A slider that mixed them would compare different things.
Terms of use. NCEI, which publishes IBTrACS, names the World Meteorological Organization’s Resolution 40 as the guide for commercial use. Using only the US agencies’ data keeps the page clear of the limits that resolution allows other agencies to set.

The wind is the storm’s maximum sustained wind: the highest one-minute average anywhere in the storm, not the wind at a given place. Over the open ocean, that number is often an estimate from satellite images of the storm’s clouds, with methods that go back to Vernon Dvorak (Velden et al. 2006). A trigger on it inherits that estimate.
A southern-hemisphere season runs from July to June, so the season 2018/19 holds Idai and Kenneth. The page covers 47 seasons, from 1979/80 to 2025/26. For the two latest, the US tracks are still provisional and will change when they are made final.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
section: From tracks to one small table
text:
From tracks to one small table
The page must answer every combination of zone, radius and wind threshold the instant a slider moves. Computing that from the tracks in the browser would be slow. So a script, scripts/showcase_trigger_lab/prepare.py, does all of it once, and the page only looks the answer up.
Hourly positions. The US agency fixes are six-hourly, and IBTrACS adds points in between, so the file has a position every three hours; the script fills in every hour by straight lines between them, but never across a gap of more than six hours (from prepare.py):
    for i in range(len(g) - 1):
        h = (t[i + 1] - t[i]) / np.timedelta64(1, "h")
        n = int(h) if 0 < h <= 6 else 1
        for k in range(n):
            f = k / n if h <= 6 else 0
            rows.append((t[i] + np.timedelta64(k, "h") if h <= 6 else t[i], *(v[i] + f * (v[i + 1] - v[i]))))
Distance to the country. For the zone “anywhere in Mozambique, within r km”, the script needs the distance from each hourly position to the country’s outline (Natural Earth, 1:50m). It flattens the Earth locally around each point, measures the distance to every segment of the outline, and keeps the smallest; inside the country the distance is zero. The script’s notes put the error of the flat approximation under 1 % for distances up to 500 km:
        c = np.cos(np.radians(py))
        ux, uy = (ax - px) * c * k, (ay - py) * k
        vx, vy = (bx - px) * c * k, (by - py) * k
        dx, dy = vx - ux, vy - uy
        t = np.clip(-(ux * dx + uy * dy) / (dx * dx + dy * dy + 1e-12), 0, 1)
        qx, qy = ux + t * dx, uy + t * dy
        out[s:s + chunk] = np.sqrt(qx * qx + qy * qy).min(axis=1)
t is how far along a segment the nearest point lies, clipped to the segment’s ends. For the six cities, the distance is the ordinary great-circle distance.
The table. For every storm and every zone, the script keeps one number per radius step (0 to 500 km in steps of 25): the strongest wind while the centre was inside. That is the whole trick:
        mw = {"Mozambique": [int(wind[dm <= r].max()) if (dm <= r).any() else 0 for r in RADII]}
97 storms came within 500 km of Mozambique with a US track. For each, seven zones times 21 radii is 147 numbers. Whether a storm triggers a cover is then one comparison: is the number for this zone and radius at least the threshold? 23 more storms came near but have no US track; they are counted on the page and left out.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
What counts as a disaster
The trigger needs a truth to be tested against: which seasons hurt. That is harder to find than the storms.
Mozambique’s disaster management institute, INGD, publishes a table of the cyclones that affected the country since the 2016/17 season, with the number of people affected, on the Humanitarian Data Exchange under CC0. The page uses it: a season counts as a disaster if INGD lists a storm in it. Each of INGD’s 13 storms is matched to a track by name and season, and the script stops if a name matches no track or more than one:
    for e in events:
        cand = [s for s in by_name.get(e["name"], []) if s["season"] in (e["year"], e["year"] + 1)]
        assert len(cand) == 1, (e, [c["id"] for c in cand])
        impacts.append({**e, "sid": cand[0]["id"], "season": cand[0]["season"]})
Before 2016/17 no open record by season was found for the page. Mozambique’s national disaster inventory for 1979 to 2012 is open on the same platform, but only as totals by year or by hazard. The other large disaster databases that were checked do not allow use on a site like this one. So 37 of the 47 seasons can show whether the trigger paid, but not whether it should have. The page marks them “no open record” and says that this is not the same as “nothing happened”.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
What ten seasons can tell
Ten seasons have an open record, 2016/17 to 2025/26. In eight of them INGD lists at least one storm. Of the other two, 2017/18 had no storm within 500 km of the country, and in 2019/20 Belna never came within 450 km and Diane came within 350 km only at 20 kt. So the record is mostly disasters, and that shapes what it can say (Figure 2).






Figure 2: What moving the wind threshold does, for two zones: how many of the 47 seasons would have paid, and how many of the 8 disaster seasons in the record it misses. The marked thresholds are where the Saffir–Simpson categories 1, 3, 4 and 5 begin (64, 96, 113 and 137 kt), and 34 kt, the lowest value of the page’s slider.



Misses are easy to see. With the page’s starting setting, anywhere in Mozambique within 100 km and 64 kt, the cover pays in 18 of 47 seasons and misses one disaster season, 2023/24 (Filipo). Raise the threshold to 96 kt and it misses four of the eight. Shrink the zone to 100 km around Beira and it misses at least six of the eight at any threshold: most of the storms that hurt Mozambique in these years did not come within 100 km of Beira.
False alarms are almost invisible. In the two seasons without a listed disaster, almost nothing came near. Within 100 km of the country, no setting gives a single false alarm. One appears only with the widest zones: Belna pays in 2019/20, without a listed disaster, for all of Mozambique within 475 km or more, or around Nacala within 500 km, at thresholds up to 100 kt. A record this short cannot tell how often a trigger pays for nothing, which is exactly what decides its price.
And the record itself is a choice. “INGD lists a storm” counts Gezani in 2025/26, with 9,040 people affected, the same as Idai in 2018/19, with 1,628,167 (INGD’s sheet for Idai may include a tropical storm of the same weeks). The page lets the reader raise the bar to 100,000 or 500,000 people, and the outcomes shift with it.
What basis risk costs the people covered is a question of its own. Clarke (2016) shows that basis risk changes demand at its root: a buyer with infinite risk aversion would rationally buy none of an index cover, and demand need not rise with risk aversion, wealth or a lower price. Jensen, Barrett, and Mude (2016) measured basis risk with eight seasons of household data for a livestock index cover in northern Kenya, and found that insured households were still left with, on average, 69 % of their original risk from high-loss events.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
What the lab leaves out
The wind is the storm’s peak, wherever it blew, not the wind at a town. Rain, rivers and storm surge are not seen at all: Idai in 2019 brought more than 200 mm of rain in a day and flooded about 3,000 km², as the page quotes from the government-led Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (2019). A season pays all or nothing, once. There is no premium, no cost and no money amount. The record of disasters covers ten seasons, and a disaster is a line in a table, not a loss. The page reproduces no real insurance product.

title: A cyclone trigger, taken apart
text:
From lab to trigger
A cover that people rely on is built differently. Real programmes calibrate on long modelled event sets as well as on history, and some trigger on a modelled loss instead of the wind, as the page notes with the example of the Caribbean risk pool’s technical paper. They pay in steps, from an attachment point to an exhaustion point, rather than all or nothing. A modelled-loss trigger weighs the hazard by where people and buildings are. And all of them need what the lab lacks most: a long, open record of losses to test against, at the scale of the zone.

title: A coastline measured from space, taken apart
text:
← Back to the Mekong coast
The Mekong showcase looks at 38 dry seasons of satellite images, 1988 to 2025, over five stretches of the delta’s coast and draws, year by year, where the vegetation ends and the mudflat begins. On the Ca Mau east coast that edge stood more than a kilometre further inland in 2025 than in the first clear years. This article takes the measurement apart: where the images come from, how a coastline is found in them, how a rate is read from 38 noisy years, and what it cannot see.
The same 9 × 9 km box on the Ca Mau east coast in the dry seasons of 1988 and 2025, as the page shows it (without its lines). Landsat images courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey.

title: A coastline measured from space, taken apart
text:
The images
Every image on the page is a Landsat image: Landsat 5 for the early years, then 7, 8 and 9. The archive has been reprocessed as Collection 2, and since then the U.S. Geological Survey provides surface reflectance worldwide, corrected for the atmosphere, as a ready product (Crawford et al. 2023). The page uses that product, called Level 2.
It reads the images through the Microsoft Planetary Computer, which offers the Landsat archive with a free, anonymous access token, and reads only the 9 × 9 km box from each scene, not the whole scene. A script, scripts/showcase_mekong/build_frames.py, asks the catalogue for every scene of a dry season over a box (from build_frames.py):
    body = {
        "collections": ["landsat-c2-l2"],
        "bbox": bbox_ll,
        "datetime": f"{year - 1}-12-01T00:00:00Z/{year}-04-30T23:59:59Z",
        "query": {"eo:cloud_cover": {"lt": MAX_SCENE_CLOUD},
                  "platform": {"in": ["landsat-5", "landsat-7", "landsat-8", "landsat-9"]}},
        "limit": 100,
    }
It looks only at the dry season, December to April. The script sorts the scenes so that Landsat 7 after May 2003, whose images have gaps from a broken scan-line corrector, comes last, then by cloud cover.

Clouds out, one picture per year
Each Landsat pixel comes with a quality band that flags fill, cloud, the margin around a cloud and cloud shadow. The script drops every pixel with any of those flags:
def clear_mask(qa: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    q = qa.astype(np.uint16)
    fill = (q & 1) > 0
    bad = (q & (1 << 1)) | (q & (1 << 3)) | (q & (1 << 4))  # dilated cloud, cloud, shadow
    return (~fill) & (bad == 0) & (q > 0)
Of the first 16 scenes of a season, it keeps up to five whose box is at least 90 % clear, preferring those with the least haze (judged by how bright the blue band is); if fewer than three qualify, it adds the clearest of the rest. From those it takes, pixel by pixel, the median. A median ignores a single bright cloud edge or a dark shadow the mask missed, as long as most looks at that pixel are clean. In practice there are fewer looks than that: on the Ca Mau east coast, the typical pixel of a clear year has two to four clean looks, and with two the median is just their mean and rejects nothing. A year counts for the measurement only if at least 85 % of the box is clear in the result. On the Ca Mau east coast, three of the 38 years fail that test: 1993, 2011 and 2012.

title: A coastline measured from space, taken apart
A coastline measured from space, taken apart
text:
A rate from noisy years
Each line now has an edge position for most clear years (35 on the Ca Mau east coast, all 38 at Ca Mau west and Soc Trang). Some years are off, for reasons such as haze or a gap the median could not fill. A straight line fitted by least squares would be pulled by such years. The page uses the Theil–Sen estimator instead, after Henri Theil and Sen (1968): take every pair of years, compute the slope between them, and keep the median of all those slopes.
def theil_sen(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Median of all pairwise slopes: a trend that a few bad years cannot drag."""
    i, j = np.triu_indices(len(x), 1)
    dx = x[j] - x[i]
    return float(np.median((y[j] - y[i])[dx > 0] / dx[dx > 0]))
Sen showed that this median slope is robust against gross errors, where least squares is not. Only lines with an edge in at least 60 % of the clear years, spread over at least 25 years, get a trend. Figure 1 shows one of them.






Figure 1: One line on the Ca Mau east coast, the one whose trend is closest to the box’s median: where its edge stood in each clear year in which it found one, with the Theil–Sen and the least-squares trend.



On this line the two methods almost agree: −30.0 against −28.7 m a year. They part where a line has a few wild years, by up to 35 m a year on some lines at Bac Lieu; there the median is the safer reading, though nothing here can prove which is right.
The rate of a box is the median over its lines; the page shows the middle half of them as the spread (Figure 2).

title: A coastline measured from space, taken apart
text:
What others measured
Anthony et al. (2015) measured the delta’s shoreline from SPOT 5 images, 2003 to 2012, and found erosion over more than half of a shoreline over 600 km long, with no identified change in the river’s discharge or in waves and wind; they find it consistent with less mud from the river, sand mining and subsidence. Tamura et al. (2020) add the long view: on the Ca Mau peninsula, the mud supply had fallen sharply by the early 20th century, after a vast network of canals was built, and the peninsula has been eroding since. Phan, Thiel de Vries, and Stive (2015) find that a mangrove belt on the eastern coast needs on average at least 140 m to stay healthy, and that sea dykes built too close squeeze it.
The page’s own numbers do not test any of this. They measure a different edge, in different boxes and years, with 30 m pixels. Where they overlap, on the muddy east coast, both see retreat.

title: A coastline measured from space, taken apart
text:
What the measurement cannot see
A dyke stops the edge. Where a dyke holds the line, the edge cannot move inland, so “no change” in front of a dyke is not “stable”. The page says this for the Bac Lieu box.
Planting looks like growth. New planting shows up as growth, as the page says.
30 m pixels. A single year’s step of less than about 30 m is noise; only the trend over decades means something.
One fixed threshold. NDVI 0.3 is a choice, the same for every year and every box. Spikes remain in the yearly chart (on the Ca Mau east coast, for example, in 2019), and their causes were not traced.
Boxes, not the coast. Five boxes of 9 × 9 km, chosen from the literature and the images, not a survey of the whole delta. The names of the boxes (“sea dyke”, “Vinh Chau”) rest on the research notes and the imagery, not on a map of the dykes.
An edge is not a sediment budget. The measurement says where the trees end, not how much mud came or went, nor why. The causes on the page come from the studies it cites, not from these images.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
← Back to Hurricane Maria 2017
The Maria showcase sends Hurricane Maria across a model of Puerto Rico’s transmission grid, hour by hour, and then holds the result up against the satellite and the outage reports. Its verdict: the model gets the direction right and misses the depth. This article takes it apart: what each piece does, the code that does it, the idea behind it, what went wrong, and what to read to go further.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
section: A screening model, held up against the record
text:
A screening model, held up against the record
The showcase does not forecast anything. It replays a storm that happened, through a model whose every piece is a first draft, and then asks how far the result is from what was measured. LiveLines, the tool behind it, calls such a comparison a record and keeps the records that miss as well as those that hit. The Maria record is a miss with a likely cause, and the most useful part of this article is the last third, on what a later look at that miss found.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
The chain
The model is a chain of small modules in the LiveLines kernel. Each takes the output of the one before (Figure 2): a grid, a storm, a rule for when lines break, a power flow, and an outcome per substation and hour. The comparison with the satellite and the reports happens outside the chain, on its last hour.






Figure 2: The chain behind the Maria page. The outcome at the model’s last hour is compared with two things measured outside the model.



The whole run is written down as one small file, a preset, so that the app and the page run the same thing: 48 model hours from 13:00 UTC on 19 September 2017, 8 runs from the seed 42. The page’s data come from a script, scripts/showcase_maria/build_data.py, that sends the preset to a locally running kernel three times (as it is, with the collapse rule on, and with it plus an over-frequency rule), re-derives the record’s scores from the answer, and stops if they differ from the record. The numbers from the run are not typed by hand: they come from the file this script writes.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
The grid
The grid comes from OpenStreetMap, turned into a network model by PyPSA-Earth (Parzen et al. 2023), an open model built on the PyPSA toolbox (Brown, Hörsch, and Schlachtberger 2018). It has 56 substations and 92 branches at 115 and 230 kV: 76 lines and 16 transformers. To it come the island’s power plants built by 2017, mostly from Global Energy Monitor’s trackers, some matched with powerplantmatching (Gotzens et al. 2019), with their status as of the trackers’ 2025 releases, and an hourly demand series (DemandCast) that PyPSA-Earth spreads over the substations.
Three things about this grid matter for everything below:

It is today’s map, not 2017’s. Of the 2,659 km of overhead line mapped in Puerto Rico, the model keeps 1,415 km.
The line ratings are standard values per voltage, not the real ones.
The plants are at nameplate: 5,666 MW of them, against 1,889 MW of load at the model’s last hour. Whether they were available in September 2017 is not in the model.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
The wind
The storm is Maria’s track from IBTrACS (Knapp et al. 2010), the US agency columns only: position, strongest wind, central pressure and the radius of strongest wind every few hours. From these a wind profile gives the wind at any distance from the centre. LiveLines uses the profile of Holland (1980) (Figure 3).






Figure 3: Holland’s profile: the wind as a share of its maximum, against the distance from the centre in radii of maximum wind. The shape parameter \(B\) sets how sharply the wind falls off outside the eyewall; LiveLines keeps it between 1 and 2.5.



The model is a few lines of algebra. With \(\Delta p\) the drop in pressure from the surroundings to the centre, \(\rho\) the density of air, \(R_m\) the radius of strongest wind and \(r\) the distance from the centre, the wind above the surface layer is, in the cyclostrophic form the kernel uses (the Earth’s rotation is left out),
\[
V_g(r) = \sqrt{\frac{B\,\Delta p}{\rho}\,u\,e^{-u}}, \qquad u = \left(\frac{R_m}{r}\right)^{B},
\]
and \(B\) follows from the track’s strongest wind and pressure drop, kept between 1 and 2.5. In the kernel (from src/kritis/chain/storm.py, shortened):
    c_lat, c_lon = at(track.lat), at(track.lon)
    dp = at(track.p_env_pa) - at(track.p_c_pa)
    rmax = at(track.r_max_m)
    vg_max = at(track.v_max_ms) / params.k_surface
    vtrans, heading = at(track.v_trans_ms), at(track.heading_deg)

    b = holland_b(vg_max, dp, params.rho_air)
    b_use = np.where(np.isfinite(b), np.clip(b, params.b_min, params.b_max), params.b_min)
    r, theta = geodesy.inverse(c_lat, c_lon, pts[None, :, 1], pts[None, :, 0],
                               a=params.wgs84_a, inv_f=params.wgs84_inv_f)
    v_g = gradient_wind(r, rmax, b_use, dp, params.rho_air)
    _, gust = surface_gust(v_g, vtrans, theta, heading, c_lat, k_surface=params.k_surface,
                           asymmetry_a=params.asymmetry_a, gust_factor=params.gust_factor)
at interpolates the track to the times wanted. surface_gust then brings the wind down to the surface (a factor of 0.9), adds up to half the storm’s forward speed on its right-hand side, where the winds of a moving northern-hemisphere storm are strongest, takes as much away on the left, and turns the result into a 3-second gust with a factor of 1.23. That factor is the cell of a WMO guideline’s table for a 3-second gust within one minute, at a coastline with the wind coming off the sea (Harper, Kepert, and Ginger 2010, Table 1.1).
Where is the wind needed? Every branch is cut into pieces of at most 10 km, and the wind is computed at the middle of each piece, twice per model hour. The hour’s value is the higher of the two.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
When a line breaks
A line does not break at one wind speed. Two towers of the same design, in the same gust, may fare differently. A fragility curve describes this as a probability: the chance that a piece of line breaks at a given gust (Figure 4).






Figure 4: The line curve the model uses, for every voltage: the chance that one piece of line breaks, against the 3-second gust. Below it, where the strongest gust on each branch falls in the Maria run.



The curve is borrowed. Raj, Bhatia, and Kumar (2021) fitted it to the transmission towers of Odisha in India after Cyclone Fani in 2019: 128 towers at 132 and 220 kV that collapsed or lost their function, out of a network of 41,814. Its median is 78.6 m/s, and it is steep: the chance rises from 1 in 100 at about 65 m/s to 99 in 100 at about 96 m/s. Hold on to that steepness; it comes back below. One more thing comes with the curve: the authors fitted it to gusts from a different wind profile (Willoughby, Darling, and Rahn 2006), scaled by their own factor, so it carries that wind model’s errors too.
The kernel draws, for every run and every piece of line, a breaking gust from that curve, and lets the piece break in the first hour its peak gust so far reaches it. A line is out as soon as one of its pieces is (from src/kritis/chain/fragility.py):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    z = rng.standard_normal((n_sample, n_point))
    cap = np.exp(np.log(median_ms[pl])[None, :] + beta[pl][None, :] * z)

    # running peak gust per point: a segment that has failed stays failed
    peak = np.maximum.accumulate(wind.gust_ms, axis=0)  # (hour, point)
    exceeded = peak[None, :, :] >= cap[:, None, :]  # (sample, hour, point)
    seg_fail = np.where(exceeded.any(axis=1), exceeded.argmax(axis=1), n_hour)

    t_fail = np.full((n_sample, n_line), n_hour, dtype=np.int64)
    np.minimum.at(t_fail, (slice(None), pl), seg_fail.astype(np.int64))
cap is the breaking gust: a normal random number \(z\), turned into a lognormal one with the curve’s median and spread. Nothing is ever repaired in this run. With the seed 42, the eight runs lose between 39 and 45 of the 92 branches. The 16 transformers are treated like lines here, with the same tower curve, and 3 to 8 of them fail per run; whether that is intended is an open question in LiveLines.
Fragility curves for power lines in storms are a field of their own. Panteli and Mancarella (2017) introduce a framework in which weather- and time-dependent failure probabilities from such curves drive a sequential Monte Carlo simulation of a power system; Panteli et al. (2017) build fragility models of components and of the whole transmission system for wind and test them on a version of Great Britain’s grid. LiveLines follows the same pattern, in a much smaller form.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
Where the power goes
Breaking lines is not yet an outage. What matters is whether power still gets from the plants to the load. The kernel answers this with a DC power flow, the linear approximation that power-system planners use when they need many answers fast. Stott, Jardim, and Alsac (2009) re-examine it and note that correct flows from it are “by no means assured”.
Each hour, the kernel does four things for every run:

Islands. It finds the groups of substations still connected by working lines.
Dispatch. In each island, the plants cover the load as far as they can. An island without a plant goes dark; one with too little serves every load the same fraction.
Flows. It solves the DC power flow in each island.
Cascade. Any line carrying more than 1.5 times its rating trips, and the kernel goes back to step 1, until nothing more trips.

The cascade is the part a picture of the network alone would miss. Hines, Cotilla-Sanchez, and Blumsack (2010) compared measures of vulnerability taken from the network’s shape with a model of cascading failure, found only a mild correlation, and concluded that judging a grid by its topology alone can mislead. In the Maria run the cascade adds up to 6 trips to the wind’s damage.
A second engine, PyPSA itself, solves the same hour as an optimisation: an ideal operator who sheds as little load as possible and never overloads a line. The page shows both; the ideal operator serves a little more here.

The rule that turns the lights off
Step 2 above has a blind spot. A real grid that is suddenly cut in two does not quietly serve what it can. If an island loses more generation than its automatic load shedding can make up, its frequency falls, plants protect themselves by tripping, and the whole island goes dark in seconds. Without a rule for this, the model reroutes power around every gap.
LiveLines has such a rule, switched off in the main run and on in two variants. An island goes dark when its sudden shortfall, measured against the load it served the hour before, exceeds a threshold (from src/kritis/chain/powerflow_dc.py):
    for isl in np.unique(label):
        buses = label == isl
        s = float(prev_served[buses].sum())
        if s <= _EPS:
            continue
        g = float(prev_gen[gen_label == isl].sum()) + float(prev_used[buses].sum())
        if s - g > threshold * s + tol_mw:
            out |= buses
The threshold is 25 %. It comes from a North American reliability standard (NERC PRC-006-5), which asks that load-shedding schemes survive an imbalance of up to that size. It is the least a scheme must survive, not a measured breaking point, and Puerto Rico is not under NERC. A second rule does the same for an island that suddenly has too much generation.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
section: Holding it up against the record
text:
Holding it up against the record
The model ends after 48 hours. Two kinds of observation are held against its last hour.

Lights at night
NASA’s Black Marble product gives the light the Earth emits at night, every day, at about 500 m, corrected among other things for the moon and for stray light (Román et al. 2018). The light is not electricity, but where a whole town’s power fails, its light goes too. Román et al. (2019) used Black Marble to follow the outage and the restoration in Puerto Rico after Maria; by their estimate, the island’s lights fell by about 80 % right after the storm.
The showcase uses the same data in a simpler way. Every land pixel on the island goes to its nearest substation. For every pixel, the normal light is the median over the clear nights before 6 September (when Irma passed north of the island). For every substation area and night, the light ratio is the light of the clear pixels that night, divided by their normal light (from LiveLines’ scripts/nightlight_bus_areas.py):
            sel = usable & has_base
            num = np.bincount(bus[sel], weights=ntl[sel], minlength=len(names))
            den = np.bincount(bus[sel], weights=base0[sel], minlength=len(names))
A night counts for an area only if at least half its normal light was seen through clear sky. From 21 September on, the first such nights were the 27th and 28th. On those two nights every one of the 50 substation areas with data was below half its normal light, and on average they kept 19 %. The model, at its last hour, still served 63 % in the same areas (a plain mean over them), and only 17 of them fell below half.


Customers without power
The U.S. Department of Energy published situation reports through the crisis. On 24 September 2017 they counted 1,569,796 customers without power: all of them. The model, at its last hour three days earlier, still served 39 % of the island’s load.
Both comparisons say the same thing. The model gets the direction right, a severe outage, and misses the depth, an island that went entirely dark. Its first explanation was on the page from the start: there is no system-wide collapse in the main run. With the collapse rule on, the areas’ mean drops to 57 %; with both rules, to 55 %. Closer, but nowhere near 19 %.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
What came later
A day after the page was built, LiveLines looked at the miss again, with a method it had used before on Typhoon Haiyan: rank the possible causes, say what each rests on, change no parameter and fit nothing. The full analysis is a record in the LiveLines repository; here is what it found, and what it means for the page.

Two errors that hide each other
LiveLines compared its wind with the gusts that weather stations on the island measured, as the National Hurricane Center’s report on Maria lists them. At the five stations whose records are not marked incomplete, the measured gust was 0.71 of the model’s (the median), and the model was 16.0 m/s higher on average. Four wind models from CLIMADA, run on the same track and the same points, were also higher, by 10.3 to 18.3 m/s on average. There is no correction for the stations’ height or exposure, and the report states no averaging time for its gusts, so this is a pointer, not a measurement of the error.
Now recall how steep the line curve is. What happens if the wind is a little weaker? The analysis ran the model with every gust scaled down:

Sensitivity runs, not proposed values. “Expected” is the sum over branches of each one’s chance to fail; served is the DC engine’s median over the eight runs. Source: LiveLines record pypsaearth_pr_maria_gap_analysis.

With a fifth less wind, almost nothing breaks. Yet Puerto Rico’s transmission lines did break, badly: Kwasinski et al. (2019) describe damage to transmission and distribution far worse than in other recent US hurricanes. So if the stations are right, the borrowed Indian tower curve is far too strong for Puerto Rico’s lines, and the model’s too-strong wind hides it. Fix one without the other and the model breaks almost no lines at all. Both must move together, from sources, and neither may be tuned to make Maria come out right.
Two of the readings behind this article point at the wind. Willoughby, Darling, and Rahn (2006) compared the most common profile functions with aircraft measurements and found that “winds near the peak are too strong” and fall off too fast away from it. And the WMO guideline whose 1.23 the kernel uses says that a “maximum 1-min sustained” wind, the kind a best track reports, is itself a gust, not a mean (Harper, Kepert, and Ginger 2010, 2); a gust factor is meant for a mean wind. Whether either explains the excess here has not been tested.


The median hid the blackouts
The collapse rule seemed to change little: the median over the eight runs barely moved. A closer look found that the largest sudden shortfall of any island of five or more substations lies between 18 % and 31 % in six of the runs, right around the 25 % threshold. With both rules on, three of the eight runs end with the island completely dark, which is what was reported, and the other five keep between 32 % and 44 % of the load. The median sits among the five. A model on a knife-edge needs its spread reported, not just its middle; showing “3 of 8 runs went dark” is now an open proposal in LiveLines.


The outage started earlier
A DOE report not used on the page says that at 07:37 UTC on 20 September, 2.6 hours before landfall, about 56 % of customers were already without power. The model still served almost all of its load then. What failed first is not known from the reports.


A different measure, a different gap
The page’s “63 % served” is a plain mean over 50 areas, and 13 of them have no load in the model, so they count as fully served. The analysis took the measure apart:

What this means for the page
The page stands as it is: every number on it comes from the run it names, and its “why it misses” says the collapse is the likely cause, not the proven one. Two things on it are now known to be incomplete. Its fragility caveat (“borrowed”) understates how much rests on the wind, and its collapse variant reports the median that hides three dark runs. Since then LiveLines has also rebuilt its night-light table so that it drops pixels on nights lit by the moon; on that table the satellite mean is 18 %, not 19 %. The page keeps the numbers of the run it names; a rebuilt page would take the new ones.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
From screening to model
What would it take before a model like this could say something about the next storm?
The distribution grid. The model stops at the substation. The lines to streets and homes, where much of Maria’s damage was, are not in it. Kwasinski et al. (2019) describe an outage that “initially affected the entire island” and lasted more than ten months, with transmission and distribution damaged far worse than in other recent US hurricanes and generation only lightly.
A tower curve from the place. Puerto Rico’s own damage records, not Odisha’s, and a curve per tower rather than per 10 km of line.
Wind checked against stations, with height, exposure and averaging time corrected, before the wind is changed.
Repair. Without repair, the model’s last hour has to stand for every later date. With it, the model could be held against the months of restoration that Román et al. (2019) followed from space.
More runs and the spread. Eight runs are enough to see a knife-edge, not to measure it.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
What the model leaves out
No distribution lines and no repair. Today’s map, standard line ratings, plants at nameplate. A tower curve from another country, applied per 10 km. A wind profile from a formula, unchecked against stations. Collapse thresholds from North American standards. Night lights as a stand-in for power. Eight runs. Every module in the chain is at placeholder maturity, and the page says so.

title: A hurricane over a grid, taken apart
text:
A reading guide
Wind in a hurricane. The profile (Holland 1980), an alternative fitted to aircraft data (Willoughby, Darling, and Rahn 2006), gusts and averaging times (Harper, Kepert, and Ginger 2010), the tracks (Knapp et al. 2010).
Grids under storms. Fragility and resilience (Panteli and Mancarella 2017; Panteli et al. 2017), a tower curve and its data (Raj, Bhatia, and Kumar 2021), why flows and not only topology (Hines, Cotilla-Sanchez, and Blumsack 2010), the DC approximation (Stott, Jardim, and Alsac 2009).
Open grid models. (Brown, Hörsch, and Schlachtberger 2018; Parzen et al. 2023; Gotzens et al. 2019).
Seeing outages from space. (Román et al. 2018, 2019).
Maria and Puerto Rico’s grid. (Kwasinski et al. 2019; Román et al. 2019).

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
← Back to LiveLines
LiveLines asks one question: when this storm passes, which transmission lines are likely to fail, hour by hour, and how much of each substation’s load can the remaining grid still serve? The Maria article takes apart the physics of one such run. This one takes apart the instrument: how it is built so that every step can be opened, every number traced, and every comparison kept honest.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
One question, one chain
LiveLines runs one calculation in six modules: place, grid, storm, fragility, power flow and outcome. The kernel runs them in the order of their cables: the grid feeds the storm module, which needs to know where the lines are. Where only the power lines are known, as in most of the world from OpenStreetMap, the chain stops after fragility: it shows which lines break, not who loses supply. Where a full grid model exists, with plants and load, it runs to the end. Every result is labelled transmission level: the model stops at the substation, and the distribution lines beyond it, where storms do much of their damage, are not in it.
Figure 1 shows how the parts fit together.






Figure 1: How LiveLines is put together. Three views show one patch; the patch runs the six modules of the kernel in cable order; the modules read their values from one register.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
Cables that check themselves
Modules do not call each other. Each one takes cables in and puts cables out: plain arrays with a fixed meaning and fixed units. The sample axis always comes first, power is in MW, positions are in degrees, hours count from the start of the storm’s window. Six cables carry everything: place, grid, wind, failures, flow and supply.
Each cable is a frozen dataclass that checks its own shapes and ranges when it is made, so a module cannot pass on something malformed. The cable that carries line failures, for example, refuses failure hours outside the window (and, in the lines cut here, repair hours before the failure) (from src/kritis/chain/contracts.py at commit b367912, shortened):
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Failures:
    """Failure hour per (sample, line). ``n_hour`` means the line never fails.
    …
    """

    t_fail_hour: IntArray
    n_hour: int
    seed: int
    t_repair_hour: IntArray | None = None
    # …
    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        _need(self.t_fail_hour.ndim == 2, "t_fail_hour: expected (sample, line)")
        _need(self.t_fail_hour.dtype.kind in "iu", "t_fail_hour: expected integer hours")
        lo, hi = 0, self.n_hour
        ok = bool(np.all((self.t_fail_hour >= lo) & (self.t_fail_hour <= hi)))
        _need(ok, f"t_fail_hour: values must lie in {lo}..{hi} (n_hour = never)")
        # … the same checks for the repair hours
A failure hour equal to the window’s length means “never fails”. That one convention lets every later module treat “out” as a simple comparison of hours.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
section: The same code, in the kernel and in the browser
text:
The same code, in the kernel and in the browser
The modules that do the arithmetic of the chain, storm, fragility, the DC power flow and outcome, are written in numpy and the standard library. That rule is what lets the same functions run in the kernel and in a visitor’s browser, through Pyodide, a build of Python for the browser (pinned to version 0.29.5 and loaded on first use). In the app, fragility, the DC power flow and outcome are the modules a visitor can edit and run in the browser; the storm module is browser-ready too, but the app takes the track and the wind from the kernel, where the track is built. A first test checks that the chain needs none of the heavy packages: it hides six of them and checks that the chain still imports (from tests/chain/test_contracts.py):
def test_chain_imports_without_heavy_packages() -> None:
    code = (
        "import sys\n"
        "for m in ('geopandas', 'pyproj', 'pandas', 'pypsa', 'shapely', 'scipy'):\n"
        "    sys.modules[m] = None\n"
        "import kritis.chain.contracts\n"
        "import kritis.chain.powerflow_dc\n"
        "import kritis.chain.geodesy\n"
        "import kritis.chain.storm\n"
        "import kritis.chain.fragility\n"
        "import kritis.chain.outcome\n"
        "print('ok')\n"
    )
    # … runs this in a fresh Python and asserts that it prints "ok"
Setting a module to None in sys.modules makes any import of it fail, so if one chain module quietly started to use pandas, this test would break. Two stronger tests go further: one compares the kernel’s results with the browser chain’s bit for bit (tests/contracts/test_browser_golden.py), and one runs the chain in a real Pyodide (viewer/tests/browser_kernel.pyodide.test.ts).
Three other engines never reach the browser. PyPSA (Brown, Hörsch, and Schlachtberger 2018), with the HiGHS solver, is the only one the kernel imports, inside one adapter: it reads the grid files and solves the second power flow, an optimum with a perfect operator. CLIMADA (Aznar-Siguan and Bresch 2019), an open platform for weather and climate risk, computes a second wind field as a cross-check; it runs in its own environment, as a separate process, and the kernel never imports it. PyPSA-Earth (Parzen et al. 2023) builds the grid models for other parts of the world, offline, also as a separate program. The rule that follows: code a visitor edits runs in their browser, or in a notebook on their own machine.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
One patch, three views
Everything a visitor chooses is one patch: a small JSON file with the modules, their knobs, the cables between them, a random seed, the number of samples, and any evidence values set for this run. The Maria showcase is one such patch (from patches/chain_maria_pr.json, shortened):
{
  "schema_version": "rack_patch.v1",
  "id": "chain.maria_pr",
  "title": "Maria 2017 over Puerto Rico, PyPSA-Earth with the 2017 plants",
  "seed": 42,
  "n_samples": 8,
  "nodes": [ … ],
  "cables": [
    {
      "id": "c_grid_storm",
      "cable_type": "grid",
      "from_port": { "node": "grid_1", "port": "out" },
      "to_port": { "node": "storm_1", "port": "grid" }
    },
    …
  ],
  "refs": []
}
The app shows the same patch at three depths. Steps puts the six modules as boxes over the map, with an hour slider. Rack shows every module with its cables, knobs and scopes, like a modular synthesiser. Code shows the chain as a live notebook (Marimo): change a setting in the notebook and the map follows, change it in the app and the notebook follows.
The same patch with the same seed gives the same numbers, bit for bit. A command-line run writes a result folder with a manifest (the patch, the code version, a hash of the evidence files, the seed, the data licences), and the same run on the same code and evidence writes byte-identical files. When the kernel runs a patch, it walks the modules in cable order and caches each module’s output under a hash of its inputs, its knobs and a fingerprint of the code and evidence, so a changed knob reruns only that module and the ones after it.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
A home for every number
No physical or economic number is meant to be typed into the chain’s own code, and review checks that none is. Every one lives in a folder called evidence/, with its unit, its source and a status. For single values the status is sourced, placeholder, or one of two others described below. A placeholder is a question, not an answer, and the app marks every result that read one. Here is one entry, the threshold of the collapse rule that the Maria showcase discusses (from evidence/params.yaml, the long fields shortened):
  powerflow.collapse_imbalance:
    value: 0.25
    unit: "1"
    distribution: {kind: deterministic, params: {}}
    source: "nerc_prc006: NERC PRC-006-5, Requirement R3. UFLS programs must meet … up to 25 percent …"
    status: placeholder
    note: "Used by powerflow_dc's collapse rule … Transferred: 25 % is the North American design basis, …"
The value has a source and is still a placeholder, because it was transferred: a North American design rule applied to an island grid that is not bound by it. The note says so.
The kernel checks these files when it loads them: a value marked sourced without a source, a missing unit or an unknown field is an error, not a warning. And every module’s result carries a trace of the values it read, so the Rack can answer “why is this number what it is?” by pointing to the entry. At this commit, params.yaml holds 157 single values: 112 are marked placeholder and 33 sourced; two more are numerical settings chosen by benchmark against an exact computation, and ten freeze an earlier model so that its old results stay reproducible. That is the honest state of a young model.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
Comparing, not tuning
LiveLines grades each module: placeholder, literature, or validated. Validated means checked against observations, with the result recorded and judged. None of the six modules is validated yet.
Two kinds of check are kept apart on purpose:

Model against model. The numpy DC power flow against PyPSA on the same inputs; the kernel’s wind against CLIMADA’s on the same track. These are comparisons. They tell how much of an answer is the choice of model, not whether the answer is right.
Model against observation. The Maria run against satellite night lights and the U.S. Department of Energy’s outage reports, recorded as comparison records. Only checks of this kind can lead to validated.

And a difference is never tuned away. It is investigated, explained if it can be, and written down. The Maria article shows what this looks like in practice: the model misses the island-wide blackout; the record says so, and a session note ranks the likely causes.
The caution has a long pedigree. Oreskes, Shrader-Frechette, and Belitz (1994) argue that numerical models of natural systems cannot be verified or validated in a strict sense, because such systems are never closed; agreement with observations confirms a model only in part. LiveLines uses “validated” in a narrower, practical sense, and keeps model-to-model agreement out of it.

When the middle hides the answer
One recent change shows why the records matter. With a collapse rule on, the eight samples of the Maria run split into two groups: some end with the island dark at transmission level (below 5 % of the load served), others keep about a third to a half of the load, and the median lies in one group only. So the outcome module now also counts how many samples end dark (from src/kritis/chain/outcome.py):
def samples_dark(share_end: np.ndarray, below: float) -> int:
    """How many samples end with a served share below ``below`` (strictly)."""
    if not 0 <= below <= 1:
        raise ValueError("samples_dark: below must be in [0, 1]")
    return int(np.count_nonzero(np.asarray(share_end, dtype=float) < below))
The threshold for “dark”, 5 %, is itself an entry in evidence/, marked placeholder: a reporting definition, not physics.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
Starting from the place
Few people know storm names. So LiveLines starts from the place: which storms passed here, how strong were they here, how often does this happen, and which would hurt the lines most?

A storm counts as near when its track came within 150 km. That radius is a setting for the list, not physics, and has no source yet.
Each storm carries the Saffir–Simpson category of its peak wind over its whole life, a label for people, not the strength at the place. The model uses the wind itself.
“Gust here” is the strongest modelled 3-second gust at the place, from the same wind code as the chain: a modelled value for sorting, not an observation.
“How often here” counts storms per decade, and one sentence counts the storms that peaked at Category 3 or above since 1980. The start year and the category are settings without a source yet. It is a count, not a return period: the record is short and the climate changes.
The ranking runs the chain up to fragility for every storm near the place, on today’s lines, and sorts by the line length that fails (the median over the samples). A storm from 1926 is run on the lines of today.

The storm tracks come from IBTrACS (Knapp et al. 2010); the wind at each line comes from the profile of Holland (1980).

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
How it is built
LiveLines is built the same way as this site: with AI coding tools, by an owner who sets the direction, tests and decides. Three habits carry most of the weight.

Decisions are written down with their reasons, and the work of each session ends in a short note: what changed, what is unverified, what is next.
Independent reviewers check a change before it counts as done: read-only reviews for the physics, for the provenance of every number and source, and for determinism (does the same patch still give the same numbers?).
Licences come first. A grid model whose licence is not settled is used for internal research only. LiveLines has such a model for the Philippines; nothing from it is shown on this site.

title: An open storm-and-grid instrument, taken apart
text:
What it cannot tell you
Transmission, not streets. A substation that keeps supply in the model can sit in an area that is dark.
Modelled, not observed. Gusts, failures and supply are modelled. Observations are kept apart and compared, never mixed in.
One curve for all lines. Every line uses one tower fragility curve fitted to one cyclone in India, applied per piece of line.
One wind model. One parametric profile, one surface factor and one gust factor for all terrain; one best track per storm. A second model (CLIMADA) runs as a cross-check only.
Two power flows, neither real. The DC flow has no operator and cascades; PyPSA has a perfect one. Reality lies between, and the model does not say where.
Not in the model at all. Rain, storm surge, flooding and landslides; trees and debris; substations and generators failing; fuel supply; people’s response; costs.

title: A mangrove coast from code, taken apart
text:
← Back to the mangrove coast
The mangrove toy shows a muddy coast with a tide, mangroves, a few animals and mud that comes and goes. This article takes it apart: what each piece does, the code that does it, the idea behind it, and what to read to go further.

title: A mangrove coast from code, taken apart
text:
A toy, not a model
Every rule in the toy was made up to look and feel right. No rule was fitted to a measurement, no number in it means anything outside the toy, and the place does not exist. That is the difference to a model. The last part is about what it would take to cross it.
The toy is still useful to me as a way in. Each of its pieces is a small, complete example of an idea from agent-based modelling or artificial life, and each one fits on a screen.

text:
Crabs, a heron, mudskippers: small state machines
The other animals each have a state and a rule for changing it. The heron has three states:






Figure 7: The three states of the heron and what moves it from one to the next. The check on the water can also end a strike.



A crab is in its hole or out of it. One line decides whether it wants to be out (from life.js):
      const want = storm < 0.2 && W < c.bh - 0.06 && Math.hypot(c.x - heron.x, c.z - heron.z) > 4;
No storm, the water below its hole, and the heron far away. Because the tide moves, the part of the shore with crabs on it grows downward as the water falls and shrinks again as it returns, without any code that says so.
A mudskipper picks, among a few random spots nearby, the one closest to the water’s edge and hops there. Each of the animals has one rule that you can read in the toy by tapping it.
This is what “agent-based” means in this article: many individuals, each with a state and a local rule, and no script for the whole. For how the approach is used in earnest, two entry points are Bonabeau (2002) on agent-based modelling of human systems and DeAngelis and Grimm (2014) on individual-based models in ecology.

text:
Sound that follows the world
Every sound is computed. Nothing is recorded.






Figure 11: How the sound is wired, simplified: the bells also reach the master and the room directly.



The sound reads the same record of the world as everything else. The water, for example, gets louder and brighter with the tide, with each wave that washes in, and with a storm (from sound.js):
      const wash = Math.pow(0.5 + 0.5 * Math.sin(env.t * 0.75), 2);     // a wave washes in every few seconds
      water.gain.setTargetAtTime(0.08 + 0.08 * tide + 0.08 * wash + 0.3 * env.storm, t, 0.3);
      waterF.frequency.setTargetAtTime(380 + 300 * tide + 250 * wash + 700 * env.storm, t, 0.3);
A slow chord changes every twelve seconds and gets darker at night. A bell melody walks up and down one five-note scale. The animals send events (a heron’s strike, the fireflies’ common beat) and the sound answers them.

title: A mangrove coast from code, taken apart
text:
From toy to model
What would have to change before any of this could say something about a real coast?
Write the model down so others can rebuild it. There is a standard protocol for describing individual-based and agent-based models (Grimm et al. 2006), known as the ODD protocol and updated twice since (Grimm et al. 2020).
Tie the rules to observations. Grimm et al. (2005) describe a general strategy for this, which they call pattern-oriented modelling.
Use what is known about the system. Models of mangrove forests exist. Berger and Hildenbrandt (2000) model the spacing, ageing and neighbourhood competition of mangrove trees; Berger et al. (2008) review the advances and limits of individual-based models of mangrove forests. For the mud, Woodroffe et al. (2016) review mangrove sedimentation and sea-level rise, Fagherazzi et al. (2012) review numerical models of salt marsh evolution, Mazda et al. (1997) study mangroves as protection from waves on a coast in Vietnam, and Winterwerp et al. (2013) define what the rehabilitation of an eroding mangrove-mud coast requires. For the Mekong Delta, Anthony et al. (2015) link rapid erosion to human activities. The toy’s rules were not derived from any of these papers. They are where I would start reading before writing a rule that claims anything.
Use a framework instead of hand-written loops once the question is serious: NetLogo (Wilensky 1999), Mesa in Python (Kazil, Masad, and Crooks 2020), Agents.jl in Julia (Datseris, Vahdati, and DuBois 2024).

title: A mangrove coast from code, taken apart
text:
What the toy leaves out
No sediment budget: mud appears and vanishes. No wave physics, no currents, no salinity. One kind of tree, with no competition for light or space beyond a minimum distance. Animals do not eat, breed or die. All rates and thresholds were set without data, to look right. The toy year has no relation to a real year.

title: A mangrove coast from code, taken apart
text:
A reading guide
Agents and individuals. The boids paper (Reynolds 1987); a model of segregation (Schelling 1971) and artificial societies grown from the bottom up (Epstein and Axtell 1996); methods and overviews (Bonabeau 2002; DeAngelis and Grimm 2014); describing and grounding a model (Grimm et al. 2005, 2006, 2020).
Synchrony. The model (Kuramoto 1975), the onset of synchronization in it (Strogatz 2000), real fireflies (Buck and Buck 1968) and pulse-coupled oscillators (Mirollo and Strogatz 1990).
Growing forms from rules. Trees and plants (Honda 1971; Lindenmayer 1968; Prusinkiewicz and Lindenmayer 1990), noise (Perlin 1985, 2002), and the chemical basis of form (Turing 1952).
Artificial life. The Game of Life (Gardner 1970), evolved virtual creatures (Sims 1994), Lenia (Chan 2019), and two overviews (Langton 1995; Bedau 2003).
Mangroves and muddy coasts, the real ones. (Berger and Hildenbrandt 2000; Berger et al. 2008; Mazda et al. 1997; Fagherazzi et al. 2012; Winterwerp et al. 2013; Anthony et al. 2015; Woodroffe et al. 2016).
Frameworks. (Wilensky 1999; Kazil, Masad, and Crooks 2020; Datseris, Vahdati, and DuBois 2024).

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
text:
← Back to Forecast
Forecast is a small game. Three crews look after a riverside town for three years, and before every round the game shows what the weather will do. This article is about the idea behind it, how it is built, and what to read to go further.

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
text:
A game, not a model
The town does not exist. Its rules were made up to make a good puzzle, no number in it has a unit, and nothing was fitted to a measurement. A flood in the game takes “one person per quarter” because that is easy to see and to count, not because floods do that.
So the game says nothing about any real place or any real forecast. What it can do is let you feel one situation from the inside: you plan with a forecast, the forecast gets worse, and nobody tells you when.

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
text:
What you do
The town is an 8 by 8 grid with a river. Each house is one person; a quarter holds up to four. A game lasts three years of five rounds.
Before each round the map shows the weather that is coming, in the order it will arrive:

a storm sweeps half a row. It takes one person in every quarter on its way and knocks down trees and levees (sandbags laid on open ground).
heat covers a square of 2 by 2 tiles. It takes one person per quarter, unless a tree stands on one of the eight tiles around the quarter.
a flood spreads from a stretch of the river, one or two tiles inland, and takes one person in every quarter it reaches.

You have three crews. Each walks up to three tiles and then works once: one lays sandbags, one plants trees, one shelters a quarter for the round. Then you end the round and the forecast comes true. Between years people move back, one per quarter that still has people.






Figure 2: Round 1 on a phone. The sandbag crew has walked next to the house the flood would take; the glowing tiles show where it can work, with a faint preview of the sandbags.



The idea of showing every threat one turn ahead comes from turn-based tactics games. A well-known example is Into the Breach (Subset Games, 2018), where every enemy shows its next attack before it lands. Forecast borrows that idea and nothing else: no names, no art, no text.

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
section: Three years, three kinds of not knowing
text:
Three years, three kinds of not knowing
The rounds look the same in every year. What changes is how much the forecast is worth.
Year 1: you know. The forecast is exact. Every tinted tile will be hit and no other. All that is left is a planning puzzle: three crews, more threats than hands.
Year 2: you know what you do not know. The forecast now gives ranges: the storm takes row 4 or row 5, the flood runs one or two tiles inland, the heat sits somewhere in a square of 3 by 3. The map shows the sure part as a solid tint and the unsure part speckled, with a question mark on the losses. The truth is always inside the range. You can still plan: cover the worst case if you have the hands, or decide which loss you can accept.
Year 3: you do not know that you do not know. One rule of the weather changes, and the game does not say so. The forecast looks as exact as in year 1, because it still runs on the old rules. A flood reaches one tile further than shown, or trees stop helping against heat, or storms take two rows. The first sign is a loss the forecast did not show, or a tile that was hit without being tinted.
The three years follow an old distinction. Frank Knight separated risk, where the odds can be measured, from uncertainty, where they cannot (Knight 1921). The work on decisions under deep uncertainty goes one step further. Lempert, Popper and Bankes use the term for situations in which analysts do not know, or the parties to a decision cannot agree on, the models that describe how the system works, the probability distributions for its key uncertainties, or how to value the outcomes (Lempert, Popper, and Bankes 2003). Year 2 of the game sits near Knight’s uncertainty: the outcomes are listed, the odds are not. Year 3 is a toy version of the deeper kind: the model itself is no longer right.
Water management has a well-known name for the assumption that breaks in year 3. Milly and colleagues describe stationarity as the idea that natural systems fluctuate within an unchanging envelope of variability, call it a foundation of training and practice in water engineering, and argue that climate change has undermined it (Milly et al. 2008). A forecast that was tuned on the old weather and is still trusted is the game’s picture of that.

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
section: What a player can try, and what the literature calls it
text:
What a player can try, and what the literature calls it
In year 3 a plan that covers the forecast exactly is the first to fail: if the flood runs one tile further, the levee stood one tile too close. Two habits are open to a player, and both have names in the literature.
The first is to stop planning for the one forecast future and to look for plans that still work when it is wrong: a tree where none is needed yet, a crew held back. Lempert, Popper and Bankes call strategies robust when they perform reasonably well across a wide range of plausible futures, instead of best in one (Lempert, Popper, and Bankes 2003).
The second is to watch for the sign that the forecast has failed and to change course when it comes. Dynamic adaptive policy pathways build this into a plan from the start: a sequence of actions over time, and signposts to monitor that show when the plan has to change (Haasnoot et al. 2013). In the game the signpost is the dashed red outline around a tile where the weather did more than the forecast said.
The game does not test either method. It only gives a few minutes in which both feel like the obvious thing to do. For the methods themselves, the open-access book edited by Marchau and colleagues is a good start (Marchau et al. 2019).

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
text:
How it is built
The game is one HTML file of about 100 KB with no library, no image files and no sound files. A short Python script puts it together from five JavaScript modules, a page template and a style sheet, about 1,700 lines in all.

One name, one town
The address of a game carries a short name, such as ?seed=k7m2p9. The name is hashed into a number that drives a small random generator, and everything follows from it: where the river bends, where the quarters lie (until at least 28 people live in town), the two first trees, where the crews start, all the weather of the fifteen rounds, and which rule will change in year 3. The same link gives the same game.
The first round is chosen when the town is made: the game looks for a stretch of river whose flood the sandbag crew can stop alone, if need be from another starting tile. In a few towns (about 3 in 100) no such stretch exists, and the first round is harder.


The forecast is the rules, run forward
There is no separate forecast. The red numbers come from running the round’s own rules on a copy of the map. In year 2 the forecast holds several versions of each hazard (two rows, four squares, two flood depths). A round in year 2 has two hazards, and the game runs every combination, eight at most. A tile that is hit in every run is drawn solid, a tile hit in some is speckled, and each quarter shows the most it could lose.
Year 3 needs only one more argument. The forecast runs the rules without the hidden change; the round itself runs them with it:
function endRound(g) {
  const hz = g.rounds[g.t];
  const guard = { shelter: g.shelter, bags: g.bags };
  const said = predict(g.terr, g.pop, hz, guard);          // what the forecast says
  const change = yearOf(g.t) === 2 ? g.change : null;      // year 3: the hidden change
  const o = resolve(g.terr, g.pop, actual(hz), guard, change);
The game then compares the two. Tiles that were hit without being named, and quarters that lost more than the forecast allowed, get the dashed outline.


How hard it is
A script played 40 towns to set the difficulty (_tools/balance.js next to this article’s source). With no crews at work, 39 % of the people are still in town after three years, on average. A simple player that moves one crew at a time to wherever the forecast loss drops most keeps 76 % (between 53 % and 107 % in single towns; more than 100 % is possible because quarters grow back between years). A person who plans the three crews together may do better. Nobody has measured how people play it yet.


Pixels and sound from code
Every sprite on the map (houses, trees, sandbags, crews) is a few rows of letters, and each letter is a colour of the day or night palette. The ground, the tints and the signs are drawn by code. This is the levee’s sandbag:
bag: ['.oooooo.', 'osssssSo', 'ossssSSo', 'oSSSSSSo', '.oooooo.'],
The map is drawn on a canvas of 344 by 208 pixels and scaled up without smoothing, so the pixels stay sharp. The ground is drawn once per town and year; water, weather, crews and houses are drawn on top in every frame. The grass gets a little drier each year.






Figure 3: Year 3 in another town. The grass has dried, and where people were lost, ruins remain. The forecast is drawn as sharply as in year 1; the dashed red outlines mark where the round before did more than it said.









Figure 4: The same game by night, with lit windows.



The music is made with the Web Audio API and reads the town like a score: a line sweeps the eight columns, each quarter with people plays a note (higher on the map, higher note; more people, louder), trees add a low tone and the river a bass. The coming weather sets the sound and the tempo, and each new year shifts the scale. In year 3 the music changes before the map shows why.


Without a mouse, without motion
Behind the canvas lie 64 ordinary buttons, one per tile, out of sight. They carry the map for keyboards and screen readers: each one says what stands on its tile, what weather is coming and what would be lost. With reduced motion switched on, the map is drawn in still frames.

title: A forecast you can trust, until you can’t
text:
What the game leaves out

Odds. Year 2 gives ranges but no probabilities, and the player never learns how often the worse end came true.
Disagreement. In the definition above, deep uncertainty is also about people who cannot agree on what a good outcome is. The game has one goal and one player.
Cost. Sandbags, trees and shelter are free; only time is short. Real protection competes with everything else a town needs.
A forecast that learns. After the first miss, a real forecaster would start to doubt the model. The game’s forecast never does.
Slow change. The rule changes once and at once. Real change is gradual, and that makes it harder to notice.

title: Haunted DAGs and spurious waffles
text:
A statistics textbook with jokes in the chapter titles. That is rarer than it should be.
Statistical Rethinking is Richard McElreath’s book on Bayesian data analysis and causal inference (CRC Press, first edition 2016, second 2020). He teaches it as a lecture course again most years and puts the lectures on YouTube for free; the 2026 run split it into a beginner and an experienced section.
The chapter titles alone are worth it: “The Haunted DAG & The Causal Terror”, “Conditional Manatees”, “God Spiked the Integers”, “Monsters and Mixtures”, and, as the last chapter, “Horoscopes”. The book opens with the golem of Prague: a statistical model is a clay creature that does exactly what it is told, with great power and no judgement. The judgement has to come from you, from a causal model of where the data came from.
My favourite example is the spurious waffles of chapter five. US states with more Waffle House restaurants per person have higher divorce rates. Nobody believes the waffles cause it, and the chapter uses it to show how to look for what is really going on. The extra joke for anyone in disaster risk: the chapter opens by noting that Waffle House is known for staying open after hurricanes, so reliably that its closures are read as a sign of how bad a storm was.
One thing I would argue with. The causal graphs in the book are DAGs, directed acyclic graphs: no loops allowed. Climate risk is made of loops. Losses change behaviour, behaviour changes exposure, exposure changes the next loss. You can unroll a loop in time, and chapter sixteen does go into population dynamics, but the acyclic picture still nudges you to think in one direction. I would keep the discipline of drawing the graph and be suspicious of the arrows that only point one way.
Three companions. Paul Wegener and Carl Boese’s silent film Der Golem, wie er in die Welt kam (1920), for the clay creature itself, in a Prague of crooked expressionist streets. Jorge Luis Borges’ story “The Garden of Forking Paths” (1941), which lent its title to one of the most useful ideas in applied statistics: Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken’s “garden of forking paths” (2013), the many small choices in an analysis that could have gone otherwise and can quietly turn noise into a finding. Read the story first; it is a spy story, and better than it needs to be. And Tyler Vigen’s Spurious Correlations, a website and then a book (2015), where the waffles would feel at home: chart after chart of unrelated things rising and falling together.

text:

title: Nausicaä, on paper
text:
If you know the film, you know the overture. Read the manga anyway. No spoilers here.
Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind ran in Tokuma Shoten’s Animage magazine from 1982 to 1994, twelve years with long pauses while Miyazaki made films, and fills seven volumes. The 1984 film came out when only the first sixteen chapters existed and covers roughly the first two volumes. The rest grew over the next ten years into something much larger and darker than the film.
The premise is simple. A world poisoned long ago. A toxic forest that keeps spreading, full of giant insects. People living at its edge, in small valleys and under empires, afraid of it. And a princess who goes into the forest to study it instead of fighting it, because she wants to understand it.
That is the part I love most. The forest is drawn as a living world, not a monster: strange, deadly, and endlessly interesting. Fear is the normal response in that world, and curiosity is the unusual one. The book takes the side of curiosity without pretending it is safe.
Then the drawing. Miyazaki drew the pages mostly in pencil, without inking, and the collected volumes are printed in brown ink. The pages are dense, almost crowded: machines, armour, clouds, crowds, plants, all in fine pencil lines, filling the panels to their edges. Next to the clean colour of the film, they look like field notes from a world that kept on existing after the camera left.
And the politics. The empires around the valley are not good or evil. Everyone has reasons, most of them bad, some of them understandable, and the story does not tidy them up for you. It is a book about people with reasons.
Some neighbours. The heroine has two sources Miyazaki named himself: the princess Nausicaa of the Odyssey, as he met her in Bernard Evslin’s small dictionary of Greek mythology, and The Lady Who Loved Insects, a Heian-period Japanese tale about a young noblewoman who would rather keep caterpillars than behave as expected. The tale is short, and worth finding.
For the drawing, the natural companion is Moebius, the French artist Jean Giraud. He and Miyazaki shared an exhibition at the Monnaie de Paris from December 2004 to March 2005, and the pairing makes sense on the page. For the forest, a much later relative: Jeff VanderMeer’s Annihilation (2014), in which a small expedition walks into Area X, a stretch of coast that nature has taken back and nobody understands. Both books ask how to look at a living place that will not behave like scenery.
Read it slowly. It rewards looking at each page longer than you need to follow the story.

text:
Connected

title: Ice, fire, jungle, voice
text: Not one film this time but all of them, or as many as I have caught. Werner Herzog, born in Munich in 1942, has made more than sixty features and documentaries, and in 2025 Venice gave him its Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. What holds them together for me is not a genre. It is a landscape at its limit, a person who goes there anyway, and a voice that refuses to pretend the landscape cares.

title: Ice, fire, jungle, voice
text:
Jungle
The early fiction is where most people start. In Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972), conquistadors go down from the Andes into the Amazon in search of El Dorado. In Fitzcarraldo (1982), which won him Best Director at Cannes, a man who wants to bring opera to the jungle sets out to haul a steamship over a mountain between two rivers. That is the premise, and I will leave it there.
Both are scored by Popol Vuh, Florian Fricke’s group. Their Aguirre album is worth hearing on its own, without the pictures, in the dark.

title: Ice, fire, jungle, voice
text:
Fire
Lessons of Darkness (1992) films the oil fires of Kuwait after the Gulf War, shortly before they were put out, as if they were the landscape of another planet. It is the most disturbing climate film I know, and it never mentions climate.
The volcano films came later. Into the Inferno (2016) he co-directed with the volcanologist Clive Oppenheimer. The Fire Within (2022) is built from more than two hundred hours of footage shot by the volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft. In the same year Sara Dosa made Fire of Love from the same archive. Watching both is a lesson in how much the cut decides: same people, same mountains, two different films.

title: Ice, fire, jungle, voice
text:
Ice
Encounters at the End of the World (2007) goes to McMurdo Station in Antarctica and finds, among the ice, the caves and the volcanoes, a community of people who ended up at the bottom of the world for reasons of their own. It is the warmest film he made, and the one I would start with.

title: Ice, fire, jungle, voice
text:
People at the edge
Grizzly Man (2005) is built largely from the footage of Timothy Treadwell, who filmed himself among the bears of Katmai in Alaska. Cave of Forgotten Dreams (2010) takes a 3D camera into the Chauvet cave in southern France. And in Ghost Elephants (2025), Steve Boyes searches the highlands of Angola for a herd that may or may not be there.

title: Ice, fire, jungle, voice
text:
The voice
In 1999 Herzog read out his twelve-point Minnesota Declaration, a short polemic against the documentary that only records facts. Its central claim is that “there is such a thing as poetic, ecstatic truth”. You can disagree with it, and I sometimes do. But it explains the films better than any review.
He also writes. The Twilight World, his first novel (German 2021, English 2022), is about Hiroo Onoda on the island of Lubang. His memoir came out in German in 2022 as Jeder für sich und Gott gegen alle and in English in 2023. Both read like the films sound.
