title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text: This one is long, because the books are.

title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text:
The object
Foundational Papers in Complexity Science is a set of four volumes from SFI Press, the Santa Fe Institute’s publisher, edited by David C. Krakauer and published over the course of 2024. It reprints 89 papers written between 1922 and 2000, each with a new introduction and annotations by present-day researchers. By the publisher’s page counts that is a little over 3,100 pages.
It is not a set you read from front to back. It is one you open somewhere in the middle and argue with.
The order is strictly chronological, and I think that is the best editorial decision in it. Papers that were never meant to meet end up as neighbours. Hayek’s “The Use of Knowledge in Society” (1945) sits two places before Shannon’s “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” (1948): one on how prices carry what no planner can know, the other on how any message can be counted in bits. Turing’s “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” (1950) is followed by Nash’s “Non-Cooperative Games” (1951) and then by Turing again, two years on, asking how pattern in a living thing could arise from chemistry alone. You would never put these on one syllabus. Side by side they look like one long conversation about how order comes out of many small parts that do not know about the whole.

title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text:
The climate book hidden inside
Nobody would sell this as a climate book. Read the contents with climate in mind, though, and one appears.

Lorenz, “Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow” (1963). Three equations for convection whose solutions never settle and never repeat. Two almost identical starting points drift apart until they have nothing in common. This is why a weather forecast has a horizon, and why climate has to be asked about in a different way from weather.
Mandelbrot, “How Long is the Coast of Britain?” (1967). The measured length of a coast depends on the length of the ruler. Every dataset of exposed coastline should carry that sentence on its first page, and almost none does.
Budyko, “The Effect of Solar Radiation Variations on the Climate of the Earth” (1969). An energy balance model with ice in it. Ice reflects sunlight, the cooling grows more ice, and past a point the feedback runs away towards a frozen planet. Tipping points, decades before the phrase became common.
May, “Will a Large Complex System Be Stable?” (1972). Two pages in Nature. Make a system larger and more richly connected at random, and beyond a threshold it becomes almost certainly unstable. The intuition that more connections mean more safety is not a law.
Holling, “Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems” (1973). Holling separates stability, how quickly a system returns to where it was, from resilience, how much disturbance it can take and still persist as the same kind of system. Much of today’s talk of resilience in adaptation plans quietly blurs the two.
Hasselmann, “Stochastic Climate Models Part I. Theory” (1976). Weather treated as random noise that the slow ocean adds up into climate variability. Hasselmann shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for the physical modelling of Earth’s climate. The other half of that prize went to Giorgio Parisi, whose 1979 spin glass paper sits a few entries further on in the same volume. I find that funnier than I can justify.
Lansing and Kremer, “Emergent Properties of Balinese Water Temple Networks” (1993). The irrigation of a whole landscape coordinated through a network of water temples, and modelled as a system whose good outcome is a property of the network, not of any one farmer or any one plan.
Ostrom, “Collective Action and the Evolution of Social Norms” (2000). The last paper in the set, on how groups manage shared things without either a state or a market doing it for them. It is a good place to end a century.

Put together, this is most of what I would want someone to have in their head before they build a climate risk model: limits to prediction, measures that depend on scale, thresholds, fragile connectivity, two meanings of resilience, noise that adds up, and institutions that work without a centre.

title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text:
Two favourites
The sandpile. Bak, Tang and Wiesenfeld, “Self-Organized Criticality: An Explanation of the 1/f Noise” (1987). Drop grains of sand onto a pile one at a time. The pile builds itself to a critical slope and then stays there, shedding avalanches of every size: many small ones, a few huge ones, with nobody tuning anything. What I love in it is the image, and one uncomfortable consequence: the grain that starts a catastrophe is an ordinary grain. The size of the trigger says nothing about the size of what follows. How much of the real world works like that is still argued about, and I do not think the argument is over. As a picture for risk it is hard to beat.
The best title. Conant and Ashby, “Every Good Regulator of a System Must Be a Model of That System” (1970). I have nothing to add to the title except that it should hang above every desk where someone manages a risk with a model they do not understand.
A smaller pleasure: Craig Reynolds’ “Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model” (1987) is in volume three, three rules that make a flock without a leader. The fish in the mangrove toy swim by those rules, as its taken-apart page explains.

title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text:
Neighbours outside the books
The set has no music in it, but complexity has a soundtrack. Steve Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians (1976): pulses and short repeated patterns for many players, and a large shape that changes so slowly you hear it arrive rather than watch it being built. Brian Eno’s Ambient 1: Music for Airports from the end of the 1970s, built from tape loops of different lengths that drift in and out of step, so the music keeps making combinations no one wrote down.
Then a game with no players: John Conway’s Game of Life, introduced to the world in Martin Gardner’s “Mathematical Games” column in Scientific American in October 1970. A grid, a handful of rules that fit on a napkin, and behaviour people are still cataloguing.
And on stage, Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia (1993), a country-house comedy whose scenes move between two centuries in the same room, with iterated equations, heat and the second law of thermodynamics in among the gossip. It is the only play I know in which an algorithm gets a laugh.

title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text:
An argument with it
My quarrel is with what the set leaves out by design. Most of the papers here are models or theory, and the best are beautiful because they are so spare: a sandpile, a random matrix, three equations. What the century of complexity science did much less often, at least in this selection, was take one of those models to a messy record of the real world and see what survived. For climate risk that confrontation is the whole job. The gap between a sandpile and a loss database is where the work is, and those volumes mostly stop at its edge.
The other quarrel is gentler. The chronological order that I praised above also hides the threads. A reader who wants to follow one idea, feedback, say, or networks, has to build the path through the volumes alone. Perhaps that is the point. It is certainly how I would want to read it anyway: with a pencil, out of order, and with a list of papers to go back to.

title: Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile
text:
What I take from it
Complexity is not a method. It is a set of warnings, each with a name and a year attached, and the most useful ones are about where our models stop. Reading the warnings in their original form, one paper at a time, is a better use of an evening than most new papers.

Mangrove coast: Its fish school by Reynolds’ three rules, with no leader.
Eilenriede fire: A grid of cells, a few made-up rules, and a chart of how often each fire size occurs: the sandpile’s question, asked of a toy.
A seagull, a butterfly, a flood: Lorenz and Arcadia again, told through the people.

title: Heatwaves and day-ahead prices: Germany, summers 2019 to 2025
text:
The question
Heat raises demand for cooling, lowers the efficiency of thermal power plants and can force them to curtail when rivers get warm. Solar output, on the other hand, peaks on the same days. Which wins in the market? This page looks at the day-ahead price, the price at which electricity for the next day is traded, for the German and Luxembourg bidding zone.

What this does not tell you

Correlation, not cause. Heat comes with other things that move prices: high solar output, low wind, plant outages, low river levels, and the same heat in neighbouring countries. This page shows what happened, not why.
A rough national temperature. Six stations stand in for Germany; regional heat is not resolved. Stuttgart-Echterdingen has no daily maximum from 3 July to 18 September 2023; on those days the mean is of the other five.
Peak hours only. The comparison uses 08:00 to 20:00 local time. Evening prices, when solar fades, behave differently.
Seven summers. That is few. One crisis year can shape the picture, which is why each summer is shown on its own.

text:
What this does not tell you

One station. Tempelhof stands for one place, not for Berlin or Germany. Urban growth around it and the end of the airport in 2008 change its surroundings.
Not homogenised. These are DWD’s measured values. Changes of instruments or siting are not corrected here.
Windows, not trends. Each 30-year window is treated as stationary. The comparison shows how much the climate shifted between them, not a forecast.
Uncertainty. Return levels for rare periods (50 and 100 years) rest on 30 maxima each and are uncertain; they are shown to make the shift visible, not as design values.

title: Water, absent
text:
Edward Burtynsky, Water (Steidl, 2013). Dams, irrigation circles, a dry lake bed, seen from far above. In many of the pictures, as the curator Russell Lord wrote of the series, the water is absent. From that height a farm looks like a painting. Only the scale tells you it was a decision.
Two companions. Godfrey Reggio’s film Koyaanisqatsi (1982): no dialogue, cities and landscapes often seen from the air or sped up, Philip Glass’s music doing the talking. And Robert Smithson’s Spiral Jetty (1970), a coil of rock built out into the Great Salt Lake. Within a few years the water covered it; drought brought it back for good in 2002, and today the shore lies far from it. A sculpture that turned into a gauge.

title: Water, absent

title: A seagull, a butterfly, a flood
text: Some writers you read for a subject. James Gleick I read for the people he finds inside one.

title: A seagull, a butterfly, a flood
text:
Chaos
Chaos: Making a New Science came out with Viking in 1987 and was a National Book Award finalist. Its material is nonlinearity, strange attractors and fractals, and the people who took them seriously early: Edward Lorenz, Mitchell Feigenbaum, Benoit Mandelbrot.
Lorenz is the one I keep coming back to. He was a meteorologist at MIT, and his 1963 paper Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow showed that a tiny, fully deterministic model of a fluid could still be unpredictable in the long run. The butterfly came later, in the title of a talk he gave in Washington in December 1972. Before that, his image had been a seagull.
For anyone who works with weather this is the founding paradox: the equations are known, and the forecast still has a horizon. I like that Gleick tells it as a story about attention, about people who looked twice at a result others would have rounded away.
The book had a second life on stage. Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia (1993) was inspired by it: one English country house, two centuries, a girl with a question about rice pudding. Read the book, then see the play, and leave the rest of the premise alone.

title: A seagull, a butterfly, a flood
text:
The rest of the shelf
Genius (1992) is his life of Richard Feynman, the second National Book Award finalist. Faster (1999) is about acceleration: atomic clocks, waiting rooms, air-traffic control. Written before smartphones, it reads now like a weather report from just before the storm. Isaac Newton (2003) keeps the alchemy next to the optics and the calculus, which is the honest way to tell it.
The Information (2011) is the big one: a history that runs from African talking drums through Babbage, Ada Byron and Morse to Shannon and Turing. It won the Royal Society Winton Prize in 2012. Pair it with Jorge Luis Borges’s The Library of Babel (1941), a story set in a library that holds every possible book, which is a joke about information and a nightmare about it at the same time.
Time Travel (2016) follows an idea rather than a science, from H. G. Wells’s The Time Machine to Gödel and Doctor Who. Its film partner is Chris Marker’s La Jetée (1962), a short told almost entirely in still photographs.
The newest, The Telephone: A New History, came out in the US this month.

title: MANIAC, twice
text: Three parts, like the book, then three neighbours and a detour.

title: MANIAC, twice
text:
One book, two languages
Benjamín Labatut is Chilean, and his earlier book, Un verdor terrible, was written in Spanish and translated into English by Adrian Nathan West as When We Cease to Understand the World. With this one he turned it around. He wrote The MANIAC in English, his first book in that language; it came out with Penguin Press in New York on 3 October 2023, and with Pushkin Press in Britain. Then he translated it into Spanish himself. Anagrama published that version as MANIAC on 25 October 2023, in its series for Spanish-language literature; its page names no other translator.
That is rarer than it sounds. A translator owes the original loyalty. An author translating himself owes it nothing, and at a press conference in Barcelona in November 2023 he said as much: translating himself let him betray himself in a way no translator would. So, in a sense, there are two originals, and the second is allowed to depart from the first. I like that idea more than I can say, and it suits a book about people who did not trust a single version of anything. If you read both languages, read a chapter or two side by side. Not to catch differences, but to watch one writer choose twice.

title: MANIAC, twice
text:
The premise
The three parts carry first names: Paul, John, Lee. Paul is the physicist Paul Ehrenfest. John is von Neumann, the longest part, made of many voices. Lee is Lee Sedol, at a Go board in Seoul in 2016, across from AlphaGo. That is all I will say about what happens. The history is public; the book’s way through it is worth arriving at fresh.
Be clear about what kind of book it is. In interviews Labatut has said his details are usually real, and that he goes close to the record and then steps back. The voices in the middle are his writing, an imagined oral history of real people, not transcripts, and reviewers have noted that he takes liberties with the lives. Read it as a novel that keeps close to the record, not as a biography.

title: MANIAC, twice
text:
Three neighbours
George Dyson’s Turing’s Cathedral (2012) is the non-fiction history of von Neumann’s computer at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton: the record that the novel goes close to and then steps back from. Greg Kohs’ documentary AlphaGo (2017) follows the people who built the program up to and through the match in Seoul. And Philip Glass and Robert Wilson’s Einstein on the Beach (1976), an opera about a scientist that tells no story about him at all, built from repetition, counted numbers and images. It is the opposite of Labatut’s method, and seeing both makes each clearer.

title: MANIAC, twice
text:
The machine, and a tangent
The MANIAC itself was a computer built at Los Alamos in the early 1950s under Nicholas Metropolis, modelled on the machine von Neumann was building at Princeton. It sits in a line of work that matters to anyone who models risk. In 1946 Stanislaw Ulam, recovering from an illness and playing solitaire, wondered whether he could estimate the odds of winning by simply playing many random games instead of doing the combinatorics. With von Neumann, Metropolis and Robert Richtmyer that became the Monte Carlo method, named by Metropolis partly after an uncle of Ulam’s who liked the casino. Its first runs, on ENIAC in 1948, were bomb physics.
Every catastrophe model that simulates ten thousand years of storms, every probabilistic loss curve, every basis risk estimate on a synthetic event set, descends from that idea: when the equations are too hard, roll the dice many times and count. The book is not about Monte Carlo. But it is about the people in whose rooms it was born, what they built, and what they thought they were doing. That makes it, to me, an uncomfortable family history of the tools risk modelling still uses.

title: MANIAC, twice
text:
Connected

LiveLines: The method, from the people around the machine: Ulam, von Neumann and Metropolis made Monte Carlo before the MANIAC was built; LiveLines draws its line failures the same way, by sampling many times.
Hurricane Maria 2017: Random runs of one storm over Puerto Rico’s grid, and how far apart they land.
Eighty-nine papers and a sandpile: Shannon, Turing and Nash in their own papers, from the same years as the MANIAC.

title: A shelf of strange books
text: A series, not a single work, and a good argument for letting a publisher choose for you now and then.

title: A shelf of strange books
text:
The series
Penguin Science Fiction launched in August 2020 under the Penguin Classics imprint, with ten books and more following. The publisher’s series page lists nineteen as of November 2026. Penguin said it wanted to challenge stereotypes about the genre, and for once the list actually does it.
What strikes me is the mix. Flatland (1884) and Vonnegut’s Cat’s Cradle are the names you expect. Around them sit books that are much less known in English: Japanese, Russian, Polish, German and Argentinian science fiction in translation, a 1931 satire on race in America, cosmic mysticism, pulp horror, robot fairy tales. Very little of it is about spaceships. Much of it is funny. A lot of it is about catastrophe, and almost none of it treats catastrophe as an action film. These are books about what people do while the world goes wrong slowly, absurdly or in plain sight.
Four to start with, chosen for range. Premises only.

title: A shelf of strange books
text:
Kobo Abe, The Ark Sakura
The shelter is ready: a disused quarry, fitted out by one man who goes by Mole, for the day the bombs fall. What it still lacks is a crew. Abe published it in Japanese in 1984; the English translation by Juliet Winters Carpenter followed in 1988, and that is the one Penguin prints.
It is the best book I know about preparedness as a state of mind. The shelter is enormous, carefully engineered and slightly ridiculous, and its builder is all three as well. Anyone who has ever planned for the worst will recognise something uncomfortable in him, and laugh anyway. If it hooks you, go back to Abe’s The Woman in the Dunes (1962) and Hiroshi Teshigahara’s film of it (1964), for which Abe wrote the screenplay: an insect collector, a village in the sand, and a premise I will leave there.

title: A shelf of strange books
section: Harry Harrison, Make Room! Make Room!
text:
Harry Harrison, Make Room! Make Room!
Written in 1966 and set in a New York of thirty-five million people at the end of the twentieth century, where water and food are rationed and everything is shared with too many others. A police detective is the thread through it.
What I like is how unspectacular it is. No single disaster, only scarcity as weather: queues, crowding, the daily arithmetic of not enough. As a forecast it got the numbers wrong. As a picture of a system running at its limit for years, it still reads well. It is in the series too.

title: A shelf of strange books
text:
Stanisław Lem, The Cyberiad
Two robot engineers, Trurl and Klapaucius, build machines for kings, for each other and for bets, across a universe that seems to be made mostly of robots. Lem published the collection in Polish in 1965; Michael Kandel’s English translation came out in 1974.
These are fairy tales for engineers, and the jokes are engineering jokes, about specifications, precision and pride. Lem’s wordplay is everywhere, and Kandel’s English version of it is a small miracle of its own. Read it for the pleasure of the language before anything else, with Kraftwerk’s Die Mensch-Maschine (1978) playing: robots, deadpan, and fonder of people than they let on. Penguin edition.

title: A shelf of strange books
section: Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, One Billion Years to the End of the World
text:
Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, One Billion Years to the End of the World
Leningrad in high summer. Malianov, an astrophysicist, has the calculation of his life on his desk, and the world will not leave him alone with it. That is as far as I will go.
The Strugatskys published it in Russian in 1976 and 1977, in a magazine; Antonina W. Bouis translated it, first under the English title Definitely Maybe (1978), and Penguin’s edition credits her translation, under a title closer to the original. It is a short book about pressure, and I think it is the best of the four. Their Roadside Picnic (1972) is not in this series, but it is the other door into their work: it became Andrei Tarkovsky’s Stalker (1979), which the brothers scripted, and book and film are different enough that both are worth having.

title: A shelf of strange books
text:
Where to go next
The rest of the list rewards wandering: Tiptree’s two collections, Gorodischer’s Trafalgar, Eschbach’s The Hair Carpet Weavers, Schuyler’s Black No More. Pick by title. That is what a series like this is for.

title: A forest fire in the city forest, taken apart
text:
← Back to the Eilenriede fire
The Eilenriede fire is a forest fire toy on the real map of Hannover’s city forest. You light fires, turn the wind, live through a dry summer, cut firebreaks and watch toy fire crews drive out. This article takes it apart: what each piece does, the code that does it, the idea behind it, and what to read to go further.

title: A forest fire in the city forest, taken apart
text:
A toy, not a model
The map is real. The forest’s outline, its paths, roads, streams and clearings, the city around it, the names on it and the fire stations all come from OpenStreetMap. Everything that happens on the map is made up. No rule was fitted to a measurement, and no number the toy shows says anything about the real forest, its fire risk or the real fire brigade. That is the difference to a model. The last part is about what it would take to cross it.
The toy is still useful to me as a way in. A forest fire on a grid is one of the oldest examples of how simple local rules make large patterns, and the questions it raises (when does a fire get through, how big do fires get) have a mathematics of their own.

section: When does a fire get through?
text:
When does a fire get through?
Light one cell in a sparse forest and the fire dies after a few cells: too many of its neighbours are empty, and too few of the trees catch. Light it in a dense, dry forest and it runs through. Between the two there is no gentle slope but a fairly sharp change.
This is percolation, studied in mathematics since Broadbent and Hammersley (1957): a medium with random gaps, and the question of whether something can get from one side to the other. In the toy two kinds of randomness meet. Whether a cell holds a tree at all is the kind called site percolation; whether a burning tree lights its neighbour is the kind called bond percolation. Dryness moves the second, the density of trees the first.
Figure 5 is computed with the toy’s own code, on the real map, without wind. For each density of trees and each dryness, 100 fires are lit at random trees, and the chart shows how much of the trees in the fire’s part of the forest one fire burns on average.






Figure 5: How much of its part of the forest one fire burns, against how many cells hold a tree, for three levels of dryness, with no wind. Each point is the average of 100 fires on the real map, run with the toy’s rules.



At dryness 0.9 the average jumps from about a tenth of the part at 55 % tree cover to about half at 65 %. At dryness 0.6 the rise comes later and is slower. At dryness 0.3 even a full forest stops most fires. The toy starts each forest at 80 % cover, so dryness decides most of what happens.
“Its part of the forest” matters here. Roads and broad gaps split the Eilenriede into 20 parts that touch nowhere, the largest 3,452 cells (about 216 ha). Without embers, a fire can never leave its part. That is a fact about the map, not about fire, but it shapes everything the toy shows.

title: A forest fire in the city forest, taken apart
text:
The storm: 300 strikes
The Storm button asks the toy’s other question: how big do fires get? It copies the forest as it is, lets lightning strike a random tree, burns that fire to the end, and does it again, 300 times, each time on a fresh copy. Every strike becomes a tiny map; when all are done, the maps sort themselves from the smallest fire to the largest, and a chart counts how often each size occurred.






Figure 6: The storm on a dry day: 300 strikes, sorted from the smallest fire (top left) to the largest (bottom right), and below, how often each size occurred, with both axes logarithmic. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL.



Figure 7 does the same with 3,000 strikes at each of two levels of dryness, 0.42 (where a summer starts) and 0.75 (after a few dry weeks), on one forest with 80 % cover and the toy’s default breeze.






Figure 7: How often fires of each size occur, from 3,000 strikes on the same forest, early and late in a summer. Both axes are logarithmic. The dashed line marks the largest part of the forest; embers can carry a fire beyond it.



Early in the summer, about a quarter of the strikes in this run stayed under 10 cells and about one in eight reached 1,000 cells or more. Late in the summer, under one in ten stayed that small and about two in three reached 1,000 cells. The single most common size is one cell, and there are fires at every size in between, which is what the logarithmic axes make visible.
Here the toy touches a real debate. Bak, Chen, and Tang (1990) proposed a forest-fire model in the context of self-organised criticality: a system that drives itself, without anyone tuning it, to a state where events of all sizes occur. Drossel and Schwabl (1992) introduced a version with a small chance of lightning and showed that it reaches such a critical state as that chance goes to zero, provided trees grow back much more slowly than forest clusters burn down. Malamud, Morein, and Turcotte (1998) found that the areas of real fires follow power laws over many orders of magnitude, and that a model of this kind behaves similarly.
The toy’s storm is not that model. It strikes a frozen forest, so what it shows is the size of the clusters a fire can reach in one forest at one moment, which is percolation again. The summer, with its regrowth and lightning, is closer in spirit to the self-organised models, but its days are short, its forest small and split into parts, and nothing in it was tested against the theory. The chart’s straight-ish stretch is a hint, not a result.

text:
Staying fast on a phone
Most of the work is small enough not to matter. Two places needed care.
The roads. In the first version of the crews, a step in which crews left could take long enough to make the picture stutter. After a rewrite (the heap written out on flat typed arrays, every station’s full field computed ahead, one by one, in quiet moments after the page has loaded, and at most one small field per step while fires burn) a full field of the 166,000 cells of the map takes about 16 ms on a desktop computer and a crew’s small field about 2 ms.
The resolution. Phones get a lower pixel density from the start and fewer points for embers, smoke and flames. If frames keep taking longer than about 1/28 of a second, the toy lowers the resolution a little, and again if needed. It stops when the tab is hidden, and visitors who ask their device for less motion get a still picture with a play button.

title: A forest fire in the city forest, taken apart
text:
From toy to model
What would have to change before any of this could say something about a real forest?
Use what is known about fire. Real fire spread is modelled from fuel, moisture, wind and slope. A widely used example is the surface fire spread model of Rothermel (1972), built on laboratory fires, with standard fuel models to go with it (Scott and Burgan 2005). FARSITE (Finney 1998) combines models of this kind to simulate how a fire grows in two dimensions. Sullivan (2009a), Sullivan (2009b) and Sullivan (2009c) survey the field from 1990 to 2007, from physical models to simulation and “mathematical analogue” models, the family the toy belongs to: models based on a mathematical idea rather than the physics of fire.
Use the right data. The toy’s classes come from map tags, not from fuel surveys. Its cell size is fixed at 25 m. It has no terrain and no fuel moisture, only one number for dryness. Its wind is the same everywhere.
Tie the rules to observations, and write them down. A model is only as good as its test against real fires. A standard way to describe such a model so that others can rebuild it is the ODD protocol (Grimm et al. 2006, 2020).
The toy’s rules were not derived from any of these. They are where I would start reading before writing a rule that claims anything.

title: A forest fire in the city forest, taken apart
text:
What the toy leaves out
No terrain, no fuel load, no fuel moisture by place, no crown fire, no smoke that matters. Time has no unit: a step is not a minute and a day is not a day. The crews have nothing to do with how a real fire brigade works, arrives or fights a fire, and the toy says nothing about any real station. The city never burns because the toy gives it no cells that can. All rates and thresholds were set by hand, to play well.
For the real fire danger on a given day, look to the weather services, not to a toy.

title: A forest fire in the city forest, taken apart
text:
A reading guide
Cellular automata and percolation. Percolation (Broadbent and Hammersley 1957) and cellular automata (Wolfram 1983).
Fires as a puzzle of physics. The forest-fire model (Bak, Chen, and Tang 1990), lightning and self-organised criticality (Drossel and Schwabl 1992), and real fires against the model (Malamud, Morein, and Turcotte 1998).
Fire spread on real ground. Cellular automata for real fires (Karafyllidis and Thanailakis 1997; Alexandridis et al. 2008); the surface fire spread model and its fuel models (Rothermel 1972; Scott and Burgan 2005); a fire area simulator (Finney 1998); a survey in three parts (Sullivan 2009a, 2009b, 2009c).
Roads and maps. Shortest paths (Dijkstra 1959), heaps (J. W. J. Williams 1964), A* (Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael 1968), OpenStreetMap (Haklay and Weber 2008).
Drawing. Mipmaps (L. Williams 1983).
Describing a model. The ODD protocol (Grimm et al. 2006, 2020).

title: Playground
text:
Small worlds made from code, for play. They are toys, not models: they follow simple rules made up for fun. The mangrove coast uses no measured data and shows no real place; the fire plays on a real map with made-up rules. For a real coast, see the vanishing coast of the Mekong Delta.


  
    
      
      Mangrove coast
      A muddy shore with a tide, mangroves that grow by rules, and animals that each follow a simple rule. Plant trees, build a dyke, take sand, send a storm or let the years run, and see what the made-up rules do to the shore. Day is drawn in ink on paper, dusk in low-poly fog, night as glowing lines. title: The vanishing coast of the Mekong Delta
text:
Showcase 3 of 4 · policy and decisions
The Mekong Delta feeds a country and keeps losing its edge to the sea. Satellites have watched it since the 1980s. Here is what they show, why it happens, and what the choice between a dyke and a mangrove belt really depends on.
How it's built →

title: The vanishing coast of the Mekong Delta
text:
See it
Every clear dry season from 1988 to 2025, five boxes of 9 × 9 km on the delta’s coast, as Landsat saw them. The bright line is the seaward edge of vegetation, mostly mangrove, found by the same rule every year. The dashed line is where it was in the first clear years.

  Where the vegetation edge stood each dry season, relative to the first clear years. Up is towards the sea (growth), down is towards land (loss). Median over the coast-normal transects that find an edge in most years; years with clouds or gaps over more than 15% of the box, or with too few transects, are left out.


How this was measured. Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9 surface reflectance, December to April (the dry season), up to five of the clearest, least hazy scenes per year, cloud and shadow removed, per-pixel median. Along transects every 90 m, the edge is the first point, coming from the sea, where the vegetation index (NDVI 0.3 or more, with bright near-infrared) stays high for 75 m. We use the vegetation edge, not the waterline: on these mudflats the waterline moves a long way with the tide, the mangrove edge does not. What it cannot see: a dyke stops the edge from moving, so “no change” in front of a dyke is not “stable”; new planting shows up as growth; pixels are 30 m, so a single year’s step of less than about 30 m is noise. The rate is a trend per transect (Theil–Sen, which a few bad years cannot drag), then the median over the transects in the box; the range shows the middle half of them.

title: The vanishing coast of the Mekong Delta
text:
Why
The coast is made of mud the river brings. Less mud arrives, the land sinks, the sea rises, and the mangroves that hold the mud are cut or squeezed. Each driver has a number, and the studies disagree, so here are ranges.

  
    Mud supply · dams
    ≈ 167 → 43–99 Mt / yr
    Suspended sediment reaching the delta. One study puts it at about 167 Mt/yr before the dams and 43 Mt/yr in 2012–2015, a 74% drop. Another finds about 99 Mt/yr still arriving at the delta's head, the loss so far mostly from dams in China, and warns that planned dams in Laos and Cambodia could halve it.
    Binh et al. 2020, Geomorphology 353; Bussi et al. 2021, Sci. Total Environ. 755.
  
  
    Sand mining
    ≈ 8–20 million m³ / yr
    Sand dredged from the rivers of Vietnam's delta, by earlier estimates; the official figure for 2018 alone is 17.8 million m³, and researchers say official numbers miss informal mining. Along the lower Mekong, about 50 million tonnes of sand a year are taken out, against about 6 million tonnes the river carries into the delta.
    Jordan et al. 2019, Sci. Rep. 9; Hackney et al. 2020, Nat. Sustain. 3.
  
  
    Subsidence
    ≈ 1–4 cm / yr
    The land sinks, much of it because groundwater is pumped. About 1.1 cm/yr on average from pumping alone, locally more than 2.5; satellite radar shows 1–4 cm/yr over large areas. The delta is on average only 0.82 m above sea level.
    Minderhoud et al. 2017, Environ. Res. Lett. 12; Erban et al. 2014, Environ. Res. Lett. 9; Minderhoud et al. 2019, Nat. Commun. 10.
  
  
    Sea-level rise
    2.2 vs 5.6–13.5 mm / yr
    At the stable gauge of Vung Tau the sea rose 2.2 mm/yr (1987–2015). At gauges on the delta coast the relative rise is 5.6 to 13.5 mm/yr: the difference is the land going down.
    Nguyen, Schwarzer & Ricklefs 2023, Estuar. Coast. Shelf Sci. 283.
  
  
    Mangroves
    ≈ 140 m belt
    On the east coast a mangrove belt needs at least about 140 m to stay healthy; dykes built too close squeeze it. But once the mud in front is gone, a wider belt does not stop the retreat. Even the global mangrove maps disagree on whether Vietnam's mangroves grew or shrank between 1996 and 2020.
    Phan et al. 2015, J. Coastal Res. 31(2); Besset et al. 2019, Estuar. Coast. Shelf Sci. 226; Global Mangrove Watch v3 and v4.1.
  


Not only the dams. Erosion on the Ca Mau coast started long before the big dams. Canals and rice fields have trapped the river’s mud on land since the early 20th century (Tamura et al. 2020, Sci. Rep. 10:8085). For 2003–2012, Anthony et al. (2015) found more than half of the delta’s shoreline, which is over 600 km long, eroding. On the 180 km muddy East Sea coast nearly 90% retreated; the mean rate there rose from about 6 m a year (2003–2007) to more than 12 m (2007–2012), with more than 50 m a year in places.

title: The vanishing coast of the Mekong Delta
text:
Decide
Hold the line with a dyke, or let a mangrove belt hold the mud? The evidence says it depends on one thing first: is there still mud in front of the coast?

  
    Mud still there, room to grow
    Mangrove belt
    Mangroves calm waves and trap mud. For small waves, up to about half a metre, a belt can be two to five times cheaper than a submerged breakwater (global review). It needs width, at least about 140 m on the east coast, and a dyke set far enough back to leave that room.
    Narayan et al. 2016, PLoS ONE 11(5); Phan et al. 2015.
  
  
    Mud gone, waves at the trees
    Fences and breakwaters first
    Where erosion has destroyed the belt, mangroves can only come back after the waves are cut. Bamboo fences do that, slow the erosion and let mud settle again; then the mangroves can be restored.
    Albers & Schmitt 2015, Wetl. Ecol. Manag. 23.
  
  
    Valuable land, no room
    Dyke
    A dyke holds a line, but a belt built too close in front of it gets squeezed. The strongest protection puts the two in series: a mangrove belt on the mudflat in front, a sound dyke behind.
    Phan et al. 2015; Albers & Schmitt 2015.
  

What it costs: we don’t show a number. We found no open, like-for-like comparison of the cost per kilometre of a dyke and a mangrove belt in the delta. The figures in the press cover different works and periods, so dividing them would mislead.
Vietnam’s government made working with nature, not against it, a guiding principle for the delta in 2017 (Resolution 120/NQ-CP, in our words). The satellite record above shows where that is hardest: where the mud has already gone.

title: Port Augusta, taken apart
text:
← Back to Port Augusta
The Port Augusta scene shows the head of Spencer Gulf in South Australia on one day, 16 October 2026: two solar farms, two wind farms and a battery, moving as the market operator’s five-minute data say they did, under the sun of that day. This article takes it apart: what each piece does, the code that does it, the idea behind it, and what to read to go further.

title: Port Augusta, taken apart
section: A real place, and what is drawn all the same
text:
A real place, and what is drawn all the same
The mangrove toy on this site is made up from the first rule to the last. This scene is the opposite case. The plants’ output, the price, the heights, the ground’s colour, the shore, the building outlines and the sun’s position are data.
Some things are still drawn, and the scene’s own info panel lists them. The hills are three times higher than life, the turbines about five times larger and the houses half again as high, so that they can be seen from 40 km away. Roof shapes, walls, windows and most building heights are made up. The sky has no clouds and no weather. The glow of a solar field and the turning of a rotor show a share of the plant’s capacity, not what a camera would see. The fine structure of the ground close up is from pictures taken between 2008 and 2010. Each part below says where the data end and the drawing begins.

section: The market, five minutes at a time

title: Port Augusta, taken apart
text:
Choosing the day
The first version replayed 20 November 2026. On that day both units of the Port Augusta Renewable Energy Park stood at 0 MW in every interval, so two of the four farms did not move. A look through the operator’s daily archive showed that they had read 0 MW since 20 October. The data do not say why. I asked for a day on which the park runs, and the scan of the archive gave 16 October: the park’s wind farm ran all day, the solar farms ran through the day, the battery both charged and discharged, and the price went below zero in the morning.
Picking a day is a choice, and it shapes the picture. A scene like this shows one day well and says nothing about the other 364.

section: Fine detail, from an older picture
text:
Fine detail, from an older picture
Ten to fifteen metres per pixel is coarse when the view comes close to a street. I found no openly licensed colour picture of this area at a finer scale. There is an older black-and-white one: Geoscience Australia’s reference image at 2.5 m, put together from pictures taken between 2006 and 2010; the mosaic used here is from 2008 to 2010.
It is older than the wind and solar farms, so it cannot replace the picture of 2026. But most of what is fine in a landscape changes slowly: creek lines, rock ledges, the street grid. So the scene takes from the old picture only what is finer than about 10 m. Each tile holds the picture divided by its own blur (from diorama_detail.py):
soft = blur(pic, BLUR_PX)
ratio = np.where(soft > 14, pic / np.maximum(soft, 1.0), 1.0)    # dark water and no-data: no detail
Close up, the shader multiplies the colour of 2026 by that pattern of lighter and darker (from shaders.js):
  if (fine > 0.0) sat *= mix(1.0, uDetRange.x + uDetRange.y * dv / max(k0 + k1 + k2 + k3, 1e-3), fine);
Putting the fine structure of a sharp black-and-white picture onto a coarser colour picture is called pansharpening; Vivone et al. (2015) compare the methods. What I do is a crude relative of it: the two pictures are from different satellites and about sixteen to eighteen years apart. Where something was built in between, the fine structure is wrong. On the solar farms the scene therefore leaves it out, and the info panel says so for the rest.
The old picture comes as one file of 410 GB in a map projection, the transverse Mercator (Karney 2011), and the script reads only the rows and columns it needs. The scene’s box is cut into 6 by 5 tiles of 4096 by 3520 pixels; the 11 tiles with the town and the plants are built, 18 MB in all, and the page fetches tiles only when the view is closer than 16 km to the ground it looks at.






Figure 6: The town from the west at 09:00: the river arm from the water outline, streets and blocks from the fine detail, houses from open outlines.

text:
Turbines, panels, battery
The 109 turbines stand where OpenStreetMap maps them, with hub height and rotor size from the same source, drawn about five times larger than life. A rotor turns faster the more its farm gives, as a share of the farm’s maximum capacity in the operator’s registration list. That is a drawing of output. It is not the real rotor speed, and the direction the rotors face is not in the data.
Bungala’s panels are listed as tracking in the registration list, so the scene turns the rows with the sun, drawn as single-axis trackers; the rows are several times wider and farther apart than real ones. A field’s glow shows its output share. The battery is eight containers; their number is a drawing, not a count. It glows blue while it takes power in and amber while it gives power out.






Figure 7: Among the turbines of Lincoln Gap at 16:30. The shadows of towers and blades are the turbine’s own shape, slid along the sun’s ray onto the ground.

What the scene leaves out
One day, chosen for the picture it gives. No clouds, no weather, no wind direction. Only the five plants with their own data are drawn; smaller solar plants nearby are left out. The scene says nothing about what a plant earns, why its output was low, or how reliable it is. Building heights, roofs and walls are mostly made up, and the Microsoft outlines were not checked one by one. The fine ground detail is about sixteen to eighteen years older than the colours. The hills, and with them their shadows, are three times too high. The picture is replayed, not live.

text:
A reading guide
The market and what storage is worth. The falling market value of wind and solar (Hirth 2013); wind and prices in South Australia (Cutler et al. 2011); the stability of the market (Simshauser 2018); the value of storage (Sioshansi et al. 2009; McConnell, Forcey, and Sandiford 2015).
Pictures from orbit. The Sentinel-2 mission (Drusch et al. 2012); Digital Earth Australia (Dhu et al. 2017) and the correction behind its pictures (Li et al. 2012); water from green and near-infrared light (McFeeters 1996); pansharpening (Vivone et al. 2015).
Heights and maps. The radar mission behind the heights (Farr et al. 2007); OpenStreetMap (Haklay and Weber 2008); simplifying lines (Douglas and Peucker 1973); the transverse Mercator projection (Karney 2011); the sun’s position (Michalsky 1988).
Shapes. Ears of polygons (Meisters 1975); the smallest rectangle around a shape (Freeman and Shapira 1975).
Drawing. Shading (Phong 1975; Schlick 1994); slopes kept in a picture (Blinn 1978); shadows (Crow 1977; Williams 1978); rings of detail (Losasso and Hoppe 2004); light for a screen (Reinhard et al. 2002).
Deciding step by step. Dynamic programming (Bellman 1954).

title: Trigger Lab: a cyclone cover for Mozambique
Trigger Lab: a cyclone cover for Mozambique
text:
How it works

Storms. Every storm since the 1979/80 season with a US-agency (JTWC) track in IBTrACS whose centre came within 500 km of Mozambique:  The whole track counts, weak and extratropical stages included. JTWC fixes are 6-hourly (3-hourly in IBTrACS); positions and winds are interpolated to hourly, gaps over 6 hours are not bridged. Mozambique is the 1:50m mainland outline, without small islands.
The trigger. A season pays if at least one storm, while its centre is inside your zone, reaches your wind threshold. One payout per season, all or nothing.
Disasters. A season counts as a disaster when Mozambique’s disaster management institute (INGD) lists a named storm in it.  Earlier seasons are marked “no open record”: no season-by-season record is used here, which does not mean nothing happened.
Seasons, not years. Cyclones here come mostly between November and April, so a season spans two calendar years. IBTrACS counts a southern season from July to June.

title: Trigger Lab: a cyclone cover for Mozambique
text:
What this does not show

Wind is the storm’s peak, not the wind on the ground. The maximum sustained wind is “the highest one-minute average wind … associated with that weather system” (NHC glossary), wherever it blows in the storm. A cover that measures wind at the site, or modelled losses, behaves differently.
Rain and floods. Damage also comes from rain, rivers and storm surge, which a wind trigger does not see. Idai (2019) brought more than 200 mm of rain in 24 hours; rivers overflowed and about 3,000 km² of land was flooded (Government of Mozambique and partners, Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, 2019).
Recent tracks are provisional. For  the US best tracks are not final yet and may change.
The missing record is part of the risk. Before  no open record found for this page says which seasons cyclones hurt. Mozambique’s national disaster inventory for 1979–2012 is open on HDX, but only as totals by year or by hazard, not cyclone disasters by season (UNDRR DesInventar via HDX, CC BY; not used here). Without such a record a trigger cannot be tested against the losses it is meant to cover. That gap is basis risk too.
Older storm records are thinner. 
 seasons is a small sample for judging a trigger. Real programmes calibrate on long modelled event sets as well as history; some trigger on modelled losses rather than wind (CCRIF, 2015).

This is an educational tool. It reproduces no real insurance product and uses only open data.
